output.text_response:
Around 1800, the land that would become Alabama was divided between two very different jurisdictions, and the records reflect that complexity. Here is the full locality guide the research agent compiled:

---

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (circa 1780–1820, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **1800:** The Alabama area was part of the **Mississippi Territory** (est. 1798). The eastern portion covering most of modern Alabama was formally added in 1804.
- **Before 1813:** The Mobile area and Gulf Coast were under **Spanish colonial authority** — a completely separate record-keeping system.
- **1817:** Congress split the Mississippi Territory, creating the **Alabama Territory**.
- **1819:** Alabama statehood (December 14).

**The critical split:** If your ancestor was near Mobile before 1813, their records are Spanish colonial records in Spanish, held in Seville or at the Library of Congress. For the interior, records fall under the Mississippi Territory government, not Alabama county governments.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **No civil birth or death registration** until 1908 statewide.
- County-level **marriage records** begin when each county was organized. Only **Washington County** (formed 1800) existed by the turn of the 19th century.
- **Church records** (especially Catholic in Mobile) are the primary vital record substitute.
- FamilySearch: [Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408) — earliest coverage for the target period.

### Church Records
- **Catholic (Mobile/Gulf Coast):** Continuous sacramental registers from the French colonial period. Held at the **Archdiocese of Mobile Archives**.
- **Methodist & Baptist:** Circuit/congregation records begin ~1808.
- FamilySearch: [Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396)
- Colonial Catholic records also at the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) and **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer** (Aix-en-Provence, France).

### Census Records
- **1800 federal census:** Negligible coverage for Alabama's portion of the Mississippi Territory.
- **1810 federal census:** First meaningful enumeration of the Alabama area.
- **Mississippi Territory censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810):** Held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History** (Montgomery). NOT available online.
- **Spanish colonial censuses** for the Mobile District: at the Archivo General de Indias and Library of Congress copies.
- FamilySearch: [Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171) covers this period.

### Probate and Court Records
- Washington County (formed 1800) has the earliest county probate records.
- FamilySearch: [Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764)
- Two **browse-only** (0% indexed) digitized volumes on FamilySearch:
  - **ImageGroup 004512889** — Territorial court and land records, 1808–1819 (214 images)
  - **ImageGroup 004512890** — Washington County deed and probate, 1803–1820 (96 images)
- Mississippi Territory court records: [Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293)

### Land Records
- Alabama is a **federal land state** — land was distributed through the U.S. General Land Office (GLO), beginning at the St. Stephens Land Office from 1803.
- **BLM GLO:** https://glorecords.blm.gov/ — search federal land patents online (free).
- Federal land **entry case files** (contain affidavits, family info): NARA, Record Group 49.
- FamilySearch: [Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694)
- Spanish/French colonial land grants: Archivo General de Indias; Library of Congress copies.

### Tax Records (Census Substitutes)
- Territorial and county ad valorem tax lists begin with county organization (Washington County from 1800).
- **Critical gap-filler** for years 1800–1809 and 1811–1819 between enumerations.
- Held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History**.

### Military Records
- Relevant conflicts: Creek War (1813–1814), War of 1812 (southern theater, 1813–1815), territorial militia.
- Service records, pension files (from 1818), bounty land warrants: **NARA** and **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/).
- Spanish colonial militia records: Archivo General de Indias.

### Other Records
- **Creek and Cherokee nation records** (NARA, RG 75): Annuity rolls and treaty records for ancestors with Native American ties.
- **Newspapers:** *Mobile Gazette* began ~1813; *Halcyon and Tombeckbe Public Advertiser* (St. Stephens) began 1818. No local papers before 1813.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives and History** (Montgomery, AL) | Territorial censuses 1801/1805/1808/1810; early tax lists; state/territorial govt. records | In-person; some finding aids at archives.alabama.gov |
| **County Courthouses** (Washington County and others) | Deed books, marriage records, probate from county formation date | In-person or written request |
| **Archdiocese of Mobile Archives** (Mobile, AL) | Sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from French/Spanish colonial period | By appointment |
| **NARA** (Washington, DC) | Federal land entry files (RG 49); pension/bounty land (RG 15); military service (RG 94); BIA records (RG 75) | In-person; ordering at archives.gov |
| **BLM General Land Office** | Federal land patents from 1803 | Free online: glorecords.blm.gov |
| **Library of Congress** (Washington, DC) | Copies of Spanish colonial records from Seville | In-person; some digital |
| **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) | Original Spanish colonial records for Mobile District: censuses, church registers, land grants, military | Written request or in-person; partial digital via PARES portal |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer** (Aix-en-Provence, France) | French colonial records for Mobile pre-1763 | Written request or in-person |
| **FamilySearch** | Multiple Alabama and Mississippi Territory collections (see above) | Free |
| **Fold3** | Military records: Creek War, War of 1812, pension files | Subscription |

---

## Records NOT Online

- Territorial census lists for 1801, 1805, 1808 (Alabama Dept. of Archives and History only)
- Spanish colonial census returns and land grants for the Mobile District (originals in Seville)
- French colonial church and civil records
- Most early county deed and tax records before 1809
- Archdiocese of Mobile sacramental registers
- Most territorial/county court minute books (except the two browse-only FamilySearch volumes)

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Mississippi Territory = pre-1817 Alabama.** Always search Mississippi Territory collections alongside Alabama ones for this period.
2. **Mobile before 1813 = Spanish colonial research.** Use the Archivo General de Indias and FamilySearch's Alabama Genealogy Wiki article: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records
3. **Federal land entry case files are the richest source.** Start at BLM GLO for the patent, then request the full case file from NARA (RG 49).
4. **Territorial census lists (1801, 1805, 1808) predate the 1810 census** — go to the Alabama Dept. of Archives and History.
5. **Tax lists substitute for missing census years** (1800–1809 and 1811–1819).
6. **County formation dates matter.** Washington County (1800) is the only county formed before 1810. Check when your ancestor's specific county was organized.
7. **Look for migration-origin records.** Settlers came primarily from Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, and Tennessee — their pre-Alabama county records may be essential.

---

If you can narrow down where in Alabama your ancestor lived — the Gulf Coast/Mobile area, the Tennessee Valley, or the interior — that will sharply focus which repositories and record sets to target first.

Note that all four `wiki_place_page` calls returned only a generic fallback page (not a specific Alabama page), and all the `wiki_read` calls for Alabama-specific topics redirected to the same generic page — I am reporting those as not found and working from what the tools actually returned. Here is the guide.

---

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (circa 1780–1820, Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Alabama achieved statehood 14 December 1819. In 1800, the present-day Alabama territory was administered as part of the **Mississippi Territory** (established 7 April 1798, carved from land ceded by Georgia and South Carolina). The eastern portion — including most of modern Alabama — was added to the Mississippi Territory by Congress in 1804. In 1817, Congress split the Mississippi Territory, creating the Alabama Territory, which became the state of Alabama in 1819.
- **County seat / administrative center:** The territorial capital was Washington, Mississippi Territory (near Natchez), then later St. Stephens (in present-day Washington County, Alabama) served as the Alabama Territory capital before Montgomery.
- **Parent jurisdictions:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), Alabama Territory (1817–1819)
- **Population during period:** Population data for this period was not returned by the tools for this standardPlace. The 1810 federal census enumerated approximately 9,000 free persons in present-day Alabama. The region was sparsely settled, with the Mobile Bay area (under Spanish control until 1813) being the largest population center.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, early cotton cultivation (which accelerated after the Creek War of 1813–1814), fur trade, and river commerce on the Alabama, Tombigbee, and Tennessee Rivers.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations across most of the interior; Euro-American settlers (primarily from Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, and Tennessee) concentrated in the northern and eastern areas; French Creole and Spanish colonial communities centered at Mobile; enslaved African Americans throughout; small numbers of free people of color, particularly in Mobile.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (concentrated in Mobile, the dominant faith during French and Spanish colonial periods); Methodist circuit riders active from around 1808; Baptist congregations forming from approximately 1808 onward; Presbyterian missions to settlers.
- **Key historical events:** French founding of Mobile, 1702; British control, 1763–1780; Spanish control of Mobile, 1780–1813; Creek War, 1813–1814 (opened much of the interior to American settlement); U.S. seizure of Mobile, 1813.

## Boundary changes

- **1798:** Mississippi Territory created, encompassing parts of present-day Mississippi and Alabama. The eastern portion (most of modern Alabama) was nominally included but largely under Creek/Cherokee control or Spanish authority.
- **1804:** Mississippi Territory extended northward to the Tennessee River, completing the legal claim over present-day Alabama.
- **Before 1813:** Mobile and its surrounding area (the Mobile District) was under **Spanish colonial jurisdiction**, not U.S. territorial authority. Records for that area before 1813 are colonial records, not American territorial records.
- **1817:** Alabama Territory separated from Mississippi Territory. Records before 1817 for present-day Alabama locations were created under the Mississippi Territory government.
- **1819:** Alabama statehood. County organization accelerated.

**Critical split:** This is a temporal split with a geographic complication. For any location in present-day Alabama before 1813 along the Gulf Coast (Mobile District), you are researching **Spanish colonial records** — not Mississippi Territory records. For interior Alabama before 1817, you are researching **Mississippi Territory records** filed at the territorial government, not Alabama records. Post-1817 county-level records begin as the Alabama Territory organized its counties. Do not assume Alabama county records exist for events before the relevant county was formed.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Alabama did not require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until 1908. Marriage records began at the **county level** when each county was organized — the earliest county in present-day Alabama (Washington County) was formed in 1800, and county-level marriage records may begin from around that date for that county. The FamilySearch Wiki's Alabama Vital Records page did not load specifically — the generic fallback returned — so no more precise date for each registration level can be cited from this survey's tool results.
- **What exists for 1800:** No statewide civil vital records. For births and deaths in this period, church records are effectively the only source. County marriage bonds and licenses begin when each county formed.
- **Where held:** County probate courts hold the original marriage records. FamilySearch has indexed county marriage records beginning from 1809 in the collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950" (collection 1598408, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408), which overlaps the target period for the earliest organized counties.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration exists for this period. Marriage coverage is sparse and county-dependent.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic church registers in Mobile for the Gulf Coast area; Baptist and Methodist circuit records for interior areas from roughly 1808 onward.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Mobile and Gulf Coast, with continuous records from the French colonial period); Methodist (circuit missions from approximately 1808); Baptist (congregations from approximately 1808); Presbyterian (from early statehood period).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (Catholic registers); membership rolls and conference minutes (Methodist, Baptist). Confirmations are a separate record series in Catholic registers.
- **Where held:**
  - Catholic records: The Archdiocese of Mobile Archives holds sacramental registers for the Mobile area, some dating to the French colonial period. The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence, France) holds French colonial records. Spanish colonial church and civil records are at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain), per the FamilySearch Wiki's Alabama Genealogy article (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records), with copies reported at the Library of Congress.
  - French records in the Mobile Municipal Archives (with microfilm copies).
  - FamilySearch has the collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950" (collection 1986396, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396), which begins in 1803 and covers the target period's later years.
- **Language:** Catholic records from the French period are in French; Spanish period records are in Spanish. American Protestant records are in English.

### Census records

- **Federal/national census:** The 1810 federal census is the first to enumerate the present-day Alabama area under U.S. authority (the territory was too sparsely settled and incompletely administered for the 1800 census to cover much of it meaningfully). The 1800 census did not enumerate the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory with any completeness. Only the 1810 census for the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory exists for the pre-statehood period.
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records). These are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History** in Montgomery.
- **Spanish colonial censuses:** Census returns for the Mobile District under Spanish administration are among the colonial records at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and the Library of Congress copies.
- **Other enumerations:** Tax lists function as census substitutes for years between enumerations.
- **Access:** FamilySearch's "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890" (collection 2016756, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756) — index only, no images (imageCount: 0). The Mississippi Territory counterpart, "Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890" (collection 1927171, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171), also covers the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory for this period; index only, no images.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories; territorial court records including land entries and oath filings.
- **Date range:** County probate records begin when each county was organized. Washington County (formed 1800) has the earliest Alabama-area county court records. The Mississippi Territory court records begin from 1798 for the territorial level.
- **Where held:**
  - County-level: County probate courts in Alabama; earliest is Washington County. FamilySearch has "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985" (collection 1537764, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764), beginning in 1809.
  - Two browse-only digitized volumes returned by `volume_search`: imageGroup 004512889 (214 images, "Territorial court and land records," 1808–1819, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable) and imageGroup 004512890 (96 images, "County deed and probate records," Washington County, 1803–1820, 0% indexed, not full-text searchable). Both must be browsed image-by-image.
  - Mississippi Territory level: "Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920" (collection 1855293, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293) covers the territorial period.
  - The Alabama Department of Archives and History holds territorial-era court records.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Alabama is a **federal land state** — land was distributed by the federal government through the General Land Office (GLO), not through the state. Land grants and patents issued by the GLO are searchable at the BLM GLO website (https://glorecords.blm.gov/). The earliest federal land entries in Alabama date from 1803 at the St. Stephens Land Office.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The federal government through the GLO; Spanish colonial grants were issued by Spanish colonial officials (records at the Archivo General de Indias and Library of Congress copies). British-era grants predate 1780 in the Mobile District.
- **Types:** Federal land entry files (cash entries, credit entries under the Land Act of 1800), original land grant patents, Spanish colonial land grants, deed records at the county level, and tax records. Bounty land warrants for War of 1812 veterans are also relevant for the period's closing years.
- **Where held:**
  - Federal land patents: BLM GLO online (https://glorecords.blm.gov/).
  - Federal land entry case files (which contain supporting documents including affidavits): NARA, Record Group 49.
  - County deed records: County courthouses. Washington County has records from 1800.
  - "Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907" (collection 1919694, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694) covers the Mississippi Territory period and includes Alabama-area entries.
  - FamilySearch also has the two browse-only volumes noted above (imageGroup 004512889, territorial court and land records, 1808–1819).
  - Spanish and French colonial grants: Archivo General de Indias (Seville); copies at the Library of Congress and Mobile Municipal Archives, per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War, 1813–1814; War of 1812 (southern theater, 1813–1815); territorial militia service; Spanish colonial militia (Mobile District, pre-1813).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files (filed beginning 1818 under the Pension Act), bounty land warrants (War of 1812 veterans), militia muster rolls.
- **Where held:**
  - Federal service and pension records: NARA (https://www.archives.gov/); also accessible via Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/).
  - Creek War and War of 1812 records: Fold3 and NARA Record Groups 15 (pension) and 94 (adjutant general).
  - Spanish colonial militia records: Archivo General de Indias and Library of Congress copies.
  - Alabama Department of Archives and History holds state-level adjutant general records.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Few organized non-religious cemeteries in this period. Private family burial grounds (often un-recorded) and church cemeteries predominate. The Old Mobile area has Catholic churchyard burials from the colonial period.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has partial coverage. Many rural burial grounds from this period are not yet recorded online.
- **Physical records:** Catholic burial registers at the Archdiocese of Mobile Archives; Protestant churches' burial records, where kept, remain at individual churches or their denominational archives.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The *Mobile Gazette* began publication around 1813 following the U.S. seizure of Mobile. No earlier regular English-language paper existed in the region. The *Halcyon and Tombeckbe Public Advertiser* (St. Stephens, Alabama Territory) began in 1818. For earlier periods, there are no locally published papers.
- **Where held:** Historical newspaper archives and the Alabama Department of Archives and History hold surviving issues.
- **Content value:** Legal notices (land sales, estate administrations), civic announcements; obituaries are rare in this very early period.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Mobile was the primary port of entry for the southern Alabama area. New Orleans (Louisiana) was a major alternative port for those arriving by sea. Atlantic ports (Savannah, Charleston) were the entry points for settlers arriving overland from the Carolinas and Georgia.
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists at Mobile and New Orleans; declarations of intention and naturalizations filed in territorial courts; Spanish colonial naturalization petitions (for the Mobile District, pre-1813).
- **Where held:** NARA holds passenger lists and naturalization records. The FamilySearch curated link to NARA (https://www.archives.gov/) is the primary access point.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed. For overland migrants, there are generally no arrival records; land entry files and territorial censuses are the first documentation.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Territorial and county ad valorem tax lists; Spanish colonial tax/tribute records in the Mobile District.
- **Date range:** U.S. territorial tax lists begin with county organization — Washington County from 1800; other areas as counties formed.
- **Where held:** Alabama Department of Archives and History (Montgomery) holds territorial and early county tax lists. Some have been transcribed and published by genealogical societies.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are critical census substitutes for years between enumerations (1800–1809, and 1811–1819 before statehood). They name heads of household and taxable property, providing a presence record when no census enumeration is available.

### Other record types

- **Spanish colonial records (Mobile District, pre-1813):** Census returns, church registers, land grants, military rosters — all in Spanish, held at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and the Library of Congress. The FamilySearch Wiki's Alabama Genealogy article (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) specifically names these repositories.
- **French colonial records (Mobile, pre-1763):** Held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence, France) and in microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives, per the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Creek and Cherokee nation records:** The Bureau of Indian Affairs records (NARA) document contacts between the U.S. government and the Creek and Cherokee nations. Some ancestors with native ancestry may appear in annuity rolls and treaty records.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (612,345 records, 306,172 images); Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (438,210 records); Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (156,789 records); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (287,634 records, index only); 2 browse-only digitized volumes for territorial period (310 images total) | Free |
| FamilySearch (via Mississippi Territory scope) | Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907 (312,450 records); Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920 (245,670 records); Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890 (198,340 records, index only); Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950 (87,654 records) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection, including 1810 census | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records including Creek War, War of 1812, pension files | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents for Alabama, beginning from 1803 (https://glorecords.blm.gov/) | Free |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records, partial coverage | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Federal records including passenger lists, pension files, land entry case files | Free to search; fees for copies |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 2 digitized volumes totaling 310 images for the 1780–1820 period. Both are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only. The total results figure was 2, meaning this was the complete digitized volume set returned, not a truncated page.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (Montgomery, AL) | Territorial census lists (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810 Mississippi Territory); early county tax records; state and territorial government records; microfilm of county records | In-person; some finding aids online at archives.alabama.gov |
| County courthouses (Washington County and others formed by 1819) | Original deed books, marriage records, probate files from county formation date | In-person or written request |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives (Mobile, AL) | Sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from French and Spanish colonial periods through statehood; oldest Catholic records in Alabama | By appointment; written request |
| Mobile Municipal Archives (Mobile, AL) | French colonial microfilm; local government records; city records | In-person |
| Library of Congress (Washington, DC) | Copies of Spanish colonial records from the Archivo General de Indias; colonial-era maps | In-person; some digital |
| NARA (Washington, DC and regional facilities) | Federal land entry files (RG 49); pension and bounty land files (RG 15); military service records (RG 94); passenger lists | In-person; online ordering at archives.gov |
| Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain) | Original Spanish colonial records for the Mobile District: census returns, church registers, land grants, military rosters — in Spanish | By written request or in-person; partial digital access via PARES portal |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (Aix-en-Provence, France) | French colonial records for Mobile, pre-1763 — in French | By written request or in-person |

---

## Records NOT online

The following exist but are not available in any online database based on this survey's tool results:

- Territorial census lists for 1801, 1805, and 1808 (held physically at the Alabama Department of Archives and History)
- Spanish colonial census returns and land grants for the Mobile District (originals in Seville; Library of Congress copies not digitized in searchable form)
- French colonial church and civil records (originals in Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives)
- Most early county deed and tax records before 1809 (the two browse-only FamilySearch volumes partially fill this gap)
- Archdiocese of Mobile sacramental registers (not in any publicly searchable online database)
- Territorial and county court minute books outside the two browse-only digitized volumes noted above

---

## Known record losses

No courthouse fires or specific record destructions for this period were named in the tool results returned by this survey. However, the period's general record sparseness is itself a survival issue: territorial record-keeping was irregular, county organization was new and underfunded, and many early settlers were not enumerated in any surviving document. The Creek War of 1813–1814 disrupted settlement and record-keeping in a significant portion of the territory. Additionally, colonial-era records are scattered across archives on three continents, and not all have been catalogued or made accessible.

---

## Research tips

- **The Mississippi Territory split is the single most important jurisdictional fact.** Before 1817, records for present-day Alabama were created under the Mississippi Territory government, not Alabama county governments. Search Mississippi Territory collections at FamilySearch alongside Alabama-specific ones. The collection "Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907" (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694) and "Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920" (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293) are primary sources for the 1798–1817 period.
- **Mobile before 1813 is a Spanish colonial research problem, not an American one.** If your ancestor was in the Mobile area before 1813, their records are Spanish colonial records — in Spanish, held in Seville or in copies at the Library of Congress. The FamilySearch Wiki's Alabama Genealogy article (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) identifies both repositories. Catholic sacramental records are the key source for vital events in that area.
- **Federal land entry files are often the richest source for early Alabama settlers.** Because Alabama is a federal land state, settlers had to file with the GLO. The federal land entry case files at NARA (RG 49) contain affidavits, correspondence, and sometimes family information. Start at BLM GLO (https://glorecords.blm.gov/) for the patent, then request the full case file from NARA.
- **Territorial census lists (1801, 1805, 1808) predate the 1810 federal census.** These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History and are the only population enumeration of Alabama-area settlers before 1810. They are not available online.
- **Tax lists substitute for missing census years.** For the period 1800–1809 and 1811–1819, territorial and county tax lists are the primary presence record. Washington County's tax lists begin from 1800.
- **The two browse-only digitized volumes on FamilySearch require image-by-image browsing.** ImageGroup 004512889 (territorial court and land records, 1808–1819, 214 images) and imageGroup 004512890 (Washington County deed and probate records, 1803–1820, 96 images) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable.
- **County formation dates control which court holds the record.** Washington County (formed 1800) is the only county in present-day Alabama formed before 1810. Baldwin County (1809), Madison County (1809), and others followed. Research your ancestor's specific location to determine which county, if any, had been organized by the event date.
- **Church records substitute for civil vital records throughout this period.** No civil birth or death registration existed. The oldest Catholic registers at the Archdiocese of Mobile Archives extend back to the colonial period and are the only vital records for that community.
- **Creek and Cherokee nation records at NARA document mixed-ancestry families.** If your ancestor may have had Native American ties, Bureau of Indian Affairs records (RG 75 at NARA) and Creek and Cherokee annuity rolls are important sources.
- **Adjoining jurisdictions:** The territory bordered Georgia (east), Tennessee (north), and Louisiana/West Florida (west/south). Settlers moving into Alabama from Georgia or the Carolinas may have left records in their origin counties. If your ancestor is not found in Alabama-area records by 1810, search the Georgia and Tennessee county records for the migration period. The Mobile District borders West Florida (Spanish until 1812), and families in the Mobile Bay area may have records on both sides of that line.

---

This guide covers Alabama, United States (pre-statehood, approximately 1780–1820). No research project file was detected at the workspace path, so no locality entry was persisted.

---

Around 1800, the land that would become Alabama was divided between Spanish colonial rule at Mobile and the new U.S. Mississippi Territory everywhere else — so your ancestor's records could be in Seville, Spain (if they were in the Mobile area before 1813), in Mississippi Territory collections on FamilySearch, in the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery, or in federal land and court records at the National Archives in Washington, D.C. The most critical warning is that Alabama county records simply do not exist yet for most of this period: only Washington County was organized by 1800, and civil registration of births and deaths was over a century away. Church records (especially Catholic ones in Mobile) and territorial census lists are your best substitutes for vital records.

If you can narrow down where in Alabama your ancestor lived — the Gulf Coast area, the Tennessee Valley, or the interior — the next step is identifying which specific county (or colonial district) would hold their records and then targeting that repository directly.

Here is the locality guide returned by the subagent:

---

**Arkansas before 1800 — Spanish Colonial Period**

*(Locality entry written as `loc_001`)*

Researching ancestors in what is now Arkansas before 1800 means working entirely within the **Spanish colonial record system**, not the state or county system that came later. The territory was a remote outpost of the **Province of Louisiana**, governed from New Orleans, with **Arkansas Post** as its only European settlement. The settlers were overwhelmingly French Creole civilians and Spanish soldiers, and the Catholic Church was the only institution recording births, marriages, and deaths.

---

### Key Record Sources

**1. FamilySearch (digitized, unindexed)**
- **Image Group 008814402** — Arkansas Post sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials), covering **1763–1800**.
- 64 images, written in Spanish, completely unindexed — must be browsed page by page.
- Use the *search-images* workflow to go through this volume.

**2. Archivo General de Indias (Seville, Spain)**
- Holds civil administration records, land concessions, military rosters, and household censuses (*padrones*).
- Accessible online via the **PARES portal** (pares.culturaydeporte.gob.es) — the best free digital starting point after the FamilySearch volume.

**3. New Orleans Notarial Archives & Louisiana State Archives**
- New Orleans was the provincial capital, so notarial and civil records flowed there.

**4. Arkansas History Commission (Little Rock)**
- Holds copies, transcriptions, and some originals of colonial-era Arkansas records.

**5. BLM General Land Office Records (post-1803)**
- U.S. land commission confirmation files frequently name **original Spanish-era grantees** and summarize the original grants — the most accessible English-language bridge into the colonial record system.

---

### Recommended Next Steps
1. Browse FamilySearch image group **008814402** (Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763–1800).
2. Search the **PARES portal** for any *padrones* or administrative records mentioning your surname.
3. Check the **BLM GLO** confirmation files for land grant references that name Spanish-era predecessors.
4. Build a focused research plan using this locality guide as its foundation.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region (Spanish Colonial Period, 1763–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Arkansas Post established 1686 by French; region placed under Spanish control by the Treaty of Paris, 1763; secretly retroceded to France in 1800 (Treaty of San Ildefonso); transferred to the United States by the Louisiana Purchase, 1803. The state of Arkansas was not formed until 1836.
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post (present-day Arkansas County)
- **Parent jurisdiction (Spanish era):** Province of Louisiana, administered from New Orleans under the Viceroyalty of New Spain.
- **Population during period:** The European settler population of the Arkansas Post was very small — measured in dozens to a few hundred — throughout the Spanish era.
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence agriculture, military garrison at the post.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish military and administrative personnel, enslaved Africans and African Creoles, surrounding Native American nations (Quapaw primarily).
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively.
- **Key historical events:** Transfer from French to Spanish control (1763); Battle of Arkansas Post (1783); retrocession to France (1800); Louisiana Purchase (1803).

## Boundary changes
- Before 1763: French Louisiana, administered from New Orleans.
- 1763-1800: Spanish Luisiana province.
- 1800: Retroceded to France.
- 1803: Louisiana Purchase, U.S. authority begins.
- Records created before 1803 do not exist in any Arkansas county courthouse — the county system had not yet been created.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- No civil vital registration existed during the Spanish colonial period.
- Catholic sacramental registers are the only vital record source for this period.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — covering European settlers, enslaved persons, and some Native Americans.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** Image group 008814402, Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial) 1763-1800, 64 images. Browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). In Spanish.
- **Where held:** Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock (originals); Arkansas History Commission (transcribed copies).
- **Language:** Spanish (some French entries pre-1763).

### Census records (padrones)
- Spanish colonial padrones (household censuses) were conducted periodically at Arkansas Post.
- Surviving padrones held at Arkansas History Commission and Archivo General de Indias.
- No digitized, indexed padrones for Arkansas Post were returned by any tool. Likely physical or microfilm only.

### Probate and court records
- Civil/legal matters adjudicated by the military commandant at Arkansas Post; records transmitted to New Orleans.
- Surviving records in Archivo General de Indias or Louisiana State Archives/Louisiana State Museum.

---

Researching ancestors in what is now Arkansas before 1800 means working entirely within the Spanish colonial record system, not the state or county system that came later. The territory was a remote outpost of the Province of Louisiana, governed from New Orleans, with Arkansas Post as its only European settlement. The settlers were overwhelmingly French Creole civilians and Spanish soldiers, and the Catholic Church was the only institution recording births, marriages, and deaths. Only one digitized source for this era is on FamilySearch: image group 008814402, a 64-image volume of Arkansas Post sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) covering 1763 to 1800. It is written in Spanish, completely unindexed, and must be browsed page by page. Beyond that single volume, the surviving colonial records are split across three major repositories: the Archivo General de Indias in Seville (civil administration, land concessions, military rosters, household censuses called padrones), the New Orleans Notarial Archives and Louisiana State Archives (because New Orleans was the provincial capital), and the Arkansas History Commission in Little Rock (which holds copies, transcriptions, and some originals). The PARES portal (pares.culturaydeporte.gob.es) is the free online gateway into the Archivo General de Indias and is the best first digital stop after the FamilySearch volume. If your ancestor held land, the post-1803 U.S. land commission confirmation files — searchable through the BLM's General Land Office website — frequently name the original Spanish-era grantees and summarize the original grants, making them the most accessible English-language bridge into the colonial record system.

The next step is to build a focused research plan using this locality guide as its foundation.

---

# Locality Guide: Ohio (pre-statehood, ~1785–1803, centered on 1790)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Ohio did not become a state until **1 March 1803**. In 1790, the area was part of the **Northwest Territory**, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. The Northwest Territory ultimately encompassed present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota. There was no state-level authority — governance was entirely federal.

By 1790, only **two organized counties** existed within what is now Ohio:
- **Washington County** (1788) — covering southeastern Ohio, seat at Marietta
- **Hamilton County** (1790) — carved from Washington County, covering southwestern Ohio, seat at Cincinnati

Everything outside those two counties was **unorganized territory** with no county-level record-keeping whatsoever.

---

## Boundary Changes

This is the central challenge for 1790 Ohio research:

1. **Before 1788:** No organized civil government under American authority existed. Any records from French or British colonial regimes must be sought in separate archives.
2. **1788:** Washington County organized — the first county in the Northwest Territory, covering an enormous area. All early southeastern Ohio settlers fell under its jurisdiction.
3. **1790:** Hamilton County organized from Washington County for the southwestern region.
4. **Post-1790:** County formation was rapid and frequent through the 1790s and into statehood. A person's records may be filed under a county that didn't yet exist when the event occurred — follow the records to the successor county or to the **Ohio History Connection** (Columbus).

Additionally, **three competing land-grant districts** create a geographic split (see Land Records below).

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Ohio had NO civil birth, marriage, or death registration in 1790.** Statewide civil registration didn't begin until 1867 for births/deaths.
- **Earliest searchable marriage records:** FamilySearch collection *"Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013"* (1.5M records) — county-level marriage bonds beginning 1789.
- **Substitute:** Church records are the primary vital-record substitute for 1790.

### Church Records
- Circuit-riding Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, and Quaker ministers were present from the late 1780s, but formal parish infrastructure was sparse.
- FamilySearch collection *"Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950"* (678,000+ records) covers this period.
- Many circuit-rider journals are in manuscript collections at historical societies, **not** in digitized databases. Absence from FamilySearch ≠ nonexistence.

### Census Records
- **1790 federal census:** The Ohio/Northwest Territory enumeration is effectively missing — settlement was thin, the frontier was dangerous, and the enumeration was incomplete.
- **1800 federal census:** The first reliably searchable census for Ohio ancestors; available free on FamilySearch and via subscription on Ancestry.
- **Recommendation:** Work *forward* from the 1800 census, then trace backward using land, tax, and military records.

### Land Records *(primary tool for 1790)*
Three distinct land systems operated simultaneously — **which repository holds a record depends entirely on where in Ohio the land was located:**

| District | Location | Primary Repository |
|---|---|---|
| **Virginia Military District** | Between Scioto & Little Miami rivers | Virginia State Library, Richmond |
| **Connecticut Western Reserve** | Northeastern Ohio | Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland |
| **U.S. Military District / Federal lands** | Remaining Ohio | BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) |

- FamilySearch collection *"Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840"* (234,000+ records) also covers this period.
- In the absence of vital records and census, a land entry is often the **first evidence** of a person's presence in a specific location at a specific date.

### Military Records
- Revolutionary War pension files are especially valuable — applicants gave sworn testimony about service, residence, family, and age. Often the richest biographical source for 1790-era Ohio ancestors. Available on Fold3 and FamilySearch.
- Bounty land warrants (Virginia Military District → Virginia State Library; federal warrants → NARA).
- Northwest Indian War (1785–1795) service records at NARA.

### Tax Records
- FamilySearch collection *"Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850"* begins in 1800 — it does **not** cover 1790.
- **Washington County tax records 1799–1803** exist as a browse-only volume on FamilySearch (ImageGroup 005112240; 73 images; 12% name-indexed). This is one of the few surviving bridges to the 1790s.
- Pre-1799 tax lists are largely physical-only at the **Ohio History Connection**.

### Probate and Court Records
- Washington County records begin 1788; Hamilton County records begin 1790.
- Court minute books often contain the only surviving record of a person's presence (road assignments, tax assessments, ordinary civil business).
- Held at the **Ohio History Connection** (Columbus) and county courthouses.

### Cemetery Records
- FindAGrave has some pioneer-era Ohio transcriptions, but 1790s coverage is thin.
- Most 1790 frontier burials were in family or church cemeteries with no formal register; county genealogical societies have compiled many transcriptions.

---

## Known Record Losses and Gaps

- **Northwest Indian War (1790–1795):** Destruction of frontier settlements caused loss of records that might otherwise have been kept.
- **No vital registration system in 1790** — many events were simply never officially recorded.
- Some early county courthouse records were lost to fire and flood in the 19th century.
- The **1790 federal census is effectively missing** for Ohio as a practical matter.

---

## Repository Guide

| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Ohio History Connection** (Columbus) | Territorial & early court/probate records; early church registers; county histories | In-person; catalog at ohiohistory.org |
| **NARA** (Washington/College Park) | Military service & pension files; territorial legislative records; naturalizations | In-person; many digitized on Fold3/Ancestry |
| **Virginia State Library** (Richmond) | Virginia Military District warrants & land records | In-person; some microfilm |
| **Western Reserve Historical Society** (Cleveland) | Connecticut Western Reserve land records | In-person; genealogical library |
| **BLM GLO** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for Ohio | Free online |
| **FamilySearch** | Marriages 1789+, Church Records 1787+, Land Records 1787+, Tax Records 1800+ | Free online |
| **Fold3** | Revolutionary War pensions; military records | Subscription |

---

## Research Tips

1. **Determine the county first:** Was your ancestor in Washington County (southeastern Ohio) or Hamilton County (southwestern Ohio)? If neither, they were in unorganized territory with no civil record-keeping.
2. **Land records are your anchor:** With no census or vital records for 1790, land grants and bounty warrants are the primary evidence of presence. Start with BLM GLO and FamilySearch's *Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840*.
3. **Three land districts = three repositories:** Identify the district before searching — the wrong repository will yield nothing.
4. **Revolutionary War pension files as biography:** If your ancestor served, their pension file may be the most detailed biographical record you'll ever find.
5. **Work forward from 1800:** Identify your ancestor in the 1800 federal census, then trace backward through tax records (1799–1803 Washington County volume), land records, church records, and military files.
6. **Ohio History Connection first for territorial records:** All records created under Northwest Territory authority, and many early county records transferred from courthouses, are held there.
7. **Church baptisms = birth records:** A church baptism is the only dated birth evidence that will exist for children born in 1790 Ohio. Search *Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950* and contact denominational archives.

---

**Summary:** Ohio in 1790 was the Northwest Territory — only two counties existed, no vital registration occurred, and the 1790 census is practically missing. The records that survive come primarily from land grants (held in three separate repositories by district), church registers, military pension files, and county court minute books at the Ohio History Connection. The most important rule: which repository holds a given land record depends entirely on *where in Ohio* the land was located.

# Locality Guide: Ohio (pre-statehood, approximately 1785-1803, centered on 1790)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Ohio became a state on 1 March 1803. In 1790, the area was part of the **Northwest Territory**, established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. The Northwest Territory ultimately encompassed present-day Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota.
- **Administrative center (territorial):** Marietta (Washington County seat), then Cincinnati (Hamilton County)
- **Parent jurisdiction in 1790:** Northwest Territory, United States — governed federally under the Continental Congress and then the U.S. Congress; no state-level authority existed
- **Population during period:** Population data for Ohio, United States was not returned by the population tool for this period, reflecting how sparse and poorly enumerated settlement was. The Wikipedia article confirms the region was thinly settled by Euro-Americans in 1790, and had large Indigenous populations (Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, Miami) for whom American governmental records were not created.
- **Economy:** Frontier subsistence farming, fur trade, military garrison economy; Revolutionary War land bounties brought many of the earliest settlers
- **Ethnic composition:** Primarily Anglo-American settlers from Virginia, Pennsylvania, and New England; some German and Scots-Irish; significant Native American population not recorded in American governmental records
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, and Quaker circuit-riding ministers; formal parish infrastructure was sparse; the Ohio History Connection and denominational archives hold what survives
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance 1787; Battle of Fallen Timbers 1794; Treaty of Greenville 1795; Ohio statehood 1803. The entire decade of the 1790s was shaped by the Northwest Indian War, which displaced settlement and resulted in the destruction of many early local records.

## Boundary changes

This is the central challenge for 1790 Ohio research and must be understood before any search begins.

**Before 1788:** The entire area now called Ohio had no organized county-level civil government under American authority. Records generated under earlier French or British colonial regimes are outside American governmental record-keeping and must be sought in separate archives.

**1788:** Washington County was organized — the first county in the Northwest Territory, covering an enormous swath of what is now Ohio and beyond. Nearly all early settlers in southeastern Ohio fell under Washington County jurisdiction. Records from this era are held at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy," [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory))

**1790:** Hamilton County was organized from Washington County, covering the southwestern portion of what is now Ohio. A settler in Cincinnati in 1790 was in Hamilton County; one in Marietta was still in Washington County.

**After 1790:** County formation was rapid and frequent through the 1790s and into statehood. A person present at one location in 1790 may find their records filed under a county that did not yet exist when the event occurred — and the successor county's courthouse holds those records, not a "Northwest Territory" archive. The rule is: determine which county held jurisdiction at the exact date of the event, trace whether that county was later subdivided, and follow the records to the successor county or the Ohio History Connection.

**Three competing land-grant districts create a geographic split:** The Virginia Military District (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers), the Connecticut Western Reserve (northeastern Ohio), and the U.S. Military District each used different survey systems and generated records in different repositories. This is a geographic split, not just a temporal one — which repository holds a given land record depends on exactly where within Ohio the land lay. See Land Records below.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Ohio did not require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until 1867 (registration was required at the county level, but compliance was inconsistent). Marriage registration began somewhat earlier at the county level but also did not exist in 1790. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Ohio Vital Records did not resolve to Ohio-specific content in this survey; the dates given here are drawn from the FamilySearch Wiki search result and the generic records overview returned — treat them as a framework to verify directly at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Vital_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Vital_Records).
- **What exists for 1790:** No civil vital registration existed. The FamilySearch collection "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013" (Collection ID 1803785, 1,523,678 records, 761,839 images) begins in 1789 and covers county-level marriage bonds and registers — this is the earliest searchable civil marriage record set for Ohio. Birth and death registration did not exist at all for this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records are the primary substitute for all vital events in 1790 Ohio. See Church Records below.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Methodist (circuit riders active from the late 1780s), Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker (particularly in southeastern Ohio); formal parishes were rare in 1790; records are scattered
- **Record types:** Baptisms (as proxy for birth dates), marriages, burials; some meeting minutes and membership lists
- **Where held:** The FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950" (Collection ID 2246917, 678,234 records, 339,117 images) covers this period and is available at [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917). Denominational archives (Methodist Conference archives, Quaker meeting records at Earlham College) hold additional material. The Ohio History Connection in Columbus is the main physical repository for early church registers that were transferred out of local congregations.
- **Language:** English
- **Caution:** Many circuit-riding ministers kept personal journals, not formal registers; these are often in manuscript collections at historical societies rather than in digitized databases. Absence from the FamilySearch collection does not mean the record does not exist.

### Census records

- **Federal census 1790:** The 1790 federal census covered the Northwest Territory, but the enumeration for the Ohio portion is extremely sparse — settlement was thin, the frontier was dangerous, and census-taking was incomplete. No Ohio 1790 schedules appear in FamilySearch's `volume_search` results for this period, which is consistent with the known coverage gap.
- **1800 federal census:** Ohio was enumerated in 1800 (still as a territory for part of the period). This is the first reliably searchable census for Ohio-area ancestors.
- **Territorial census:** No separate Ohio territorial census is documented in the FamilySearch collections returned for this period.
- **Access:** The 1800 census for Ohio is indexed and available on Ancestry (subscription) and FamilySearch (free). The 1790 coverage gap should be assumed unless a specific entry is confirmed.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories; territorial court records (General Court of the Northwest Territory, then county courts of common pleas after 1788)
- **Date range:** Washington County records begin 1788; Hamilton County records begin 1790
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection (Columbus) holds the bulk of territorial-era probate and court records. County courthouses hold records created after each county's formation. Physical only for most territorial records; some have been microfilmed.
- **Note:** Court minute books from this era often contain the only surviving record of a person's presence in a county — road maintenance assignments, poor relief, tax assessments, and ordinary civil business.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Ohio is a federal-land state, but three distinct systems operated within it simultaneously, each with its own record trail:
  1. **Virginia Military District** (Scioto to Little Miami rivers): metes-and-bounds survey; warrants held at the Virginia State Library in Richmond; these were land bounties granted to Virginia Revolutionary War veterans.
  2. **Connecticut Western Reserve** (northeastern Ohio): rectangular survey on a different grid; records at the Western Reserve Historical Society in Cleveland.
  3. **U.S. Military District and general federal lands**: General Land Office patents, accessible at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (GLO) website (glorecords.blm.gov), which covers Ohio federal land patents.
- **Which repository holds a given record depends on where in Ohio the land was located** — this is a geographic split. Do not assume a single repository covers all Ohio land records of this era; determine the district first. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy — Land Records," [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records))
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840" (Collection ID 1542187, 234,567 records, 117,283 images): [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187). This collection begins in 1787 and directly covers the target period.
- **Types:** Grants, patents, deeds, entries, surveys
- **Substitute value:** In the absence of vital records and census, a land entry is often the first evidence of a person's presence in a specific Ohio location at a specific date.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Northwest Indian War (1785-1795); American Revolutionary War bounty land claims bring many settlers into the record
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files for the Revolutionary War period (at NARA); bounty land warrants (Virginia Military District warrants at Virginia State Library; federal bounty land warrants at NARA); Northwest Indian War service records at NARA
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and its digitized collections); Fold3.com (subscription) has many pension files indexed; the Ohio History Connection holds state militia records
- **Note:** Revolutionary War pension files are particularly valuable for 1790-era Ohio ancestors because applicants gave sworn testimony about their service, residence, family, and age. Many pension files are online at Fold3 and FamilySearch.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Territorial and county property/poll tax lists
- **Date range:** The FamilySearch collection "Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850" (Collection ID 1987542, 345,890 records, 172,945 images) begins in 1800, not 1790. This means the collection does not cover the target year.
- **Pre-1800 tax records:** `volume_search` returned one volume of Washington County tax records covering 1799-1803 (imageGroupNumber 005112240; 73 images; 12% name-indexed, not full-text searchable), held as browse-only with partial indexing. Pre-1799 tax lists for the Northwest Territory are largely physical-only at the Ohio History Connection.
- **Substitute value:** For the gap between 1790 and 1800, tax lists are the primary substitute for missing census and vital records. The 1799-1803 Washington County volume at FamilySearch should be browsed for early Washington County settlers.

### Cemetery records

- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com, free) has transcriptions of many Ohio pioneer-era graves. Coverage for 1790s burials is thinner than for later periods.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for 1790 are rare; most frontier burials were in family cemeteries or church graveyards with no formal register. The Ohio History Connection and county genealogical societies have compiled many early cemetery transcriptions.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Centinel of the North-Western Territory (Cincinnati, 1793) was among the earliest Ohio newspapers, postdating 1790 by three years. For events in 1790 itself, no local Ohio newspaper existed.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription) and the Ohio History Connection's digital newspaper archive hold what survives. Coverage for the 1790s is very sparse.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Most settlers reaching Ohio in 1790 came overland from Virginia, Pennsylvania, and New England — not by sea. Immigration records in the traditional sense (passenger lists) are not the primary tool here.
- **Naturalization:** Naturalization records for this period are at the county court of common pleas. Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record; Washington County and Hamilton County court records are the starting points. NARA holds some territorial-era naturalization records.
- **Declarations of intention and affidavits** filed inland by immigrant settlers are held at the Ohio History Connection and county courthouses.

### Other record types

- **Town and county histories:** Ohio was extensively documented in 19th-century county histories, many of which reprint early records and biographical sketches of pioneer families. These are often the only surviving transcription of records since lost. WorldCat and the FamilySearch Catalog are the finding tools.
- **Territorial legislative records:** The Northwest Territory's legislative proceedings (1788-1803) are at NARA and name landowners, officeholders, and petitioners.
- **Bible and family records:** Pioneer families in Ohio kept family Bibles recording births, marriages, and deaths with no civil equivalent. The Ohio Genealogical Society and county chapters hold many donated Bible records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Ohio, County Marriages, 1789-2013 (1,523,678 records); Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950 (678,234 records); Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840 (234,567 records); Ohio, Tax Records, 1800-1850 (345,890 records); Washington County tax volume 1799-1803 (browse-only, 12% indexed) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection including 1800 Ohio; various Ohio collections | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files; military service records | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (very sparse for 1790s Ohio) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for Ohio | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Territorial records, naturalization, military | Free to access finding aids; some digitized |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned a total of 2 digitized volumes matching Ohio in the 1780-1810 window. Both are detailed above. `collections_search` returned 5 collections. These represent the complete returned sets for this query.

**Note on wiki pages:** All four `wiki_place_page` calls (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) for Ohio returned only a generic "Genealogy Research Guide" page rather than Ohio-specific content, and all five constructed-URL `wiki_read` calls for Ohio-specific pages (Ohio_Vital_Records, Ohio_Land_and_Property, Ohio_Church_Records, Ohio_Census, Ohio_Genealogy, Northwest_Territory_Genealogy) resolved to the same generic "Genealogy Records" page. The specific Ohio details cited in this guide come from the `wiki_search` results, which returned two high-relevance chunks from the FamilySearch "Ohio Genealogy" page. The researcher should consult [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy) directly for the most current detail.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Ohio History Connection (Columbus, OH) | Territorial and early state records; court and probate records from Washington and Hamilton Counties; early church registers; county histories; newspaper archives | In-person; online catalog at ohiohistory.org |
| NARA (Washington, D.C. / College Park) | Territorial legislative records; military service and pension files; pre-1906 naturalizations; some territorial land records | In-person; many records digitized on Fold3 and Ancestry |
| Virginia State Library (Richmond, VA) | Virginia Military District warrants and land records for southwestern Ohio | In-person; some microfilm available |
| Western Reserve Historical Society (Cleveland, OH) | Connecticut Western Reserve land records; northeastern Ohio records | In-person; genealogical library open to researchers |
| County courthouses (Washington Co./Marietta; Hamilton Co./Cincinnati) | Deed books, court records from county formation dates; some transferred to Ohio History Connection | In-person or mail |
| Ohio Genealogical Society (Morrow, OH) | Bible records, surname files, county genealogical publications | In-person; county chapter collections vary |

## Records NOT online

The following record types exist for pre-statehood Ohio but are not available in any online database as of this survey:

- Pre-1799 county tax lists (physical at Ohio History Connection)
- Territorial legislative and administrative records (physical at NARA; some microfilmed)
- Most circuit-riding minister journals and manuscript baptism/marriage records (at denominational archives and historical societies)
- Family Bible records donated to local genealogical society chapters
- Virginia Military District warrant files prior to any digitization by the Virginia State Library (verify current status directly with that library)
- Early Washington County and Hamilton County court minute books (some microfilmed; verify with Ohio History Connection)

## Known record losses

- The **Northwest Indian War (1790-1795)** resulted in destruction or abandonment of frontier settlements, which means records that might have been created were often not kept or were lost during evacuations.
- The frontier infrastructure of 1790 meant civil record-keeping was thin by design — no vital registration system existed, and many events were simply never officially recorded.
- Some early county courthouse records were lost to fire and flood in the 19th century; verify the specific county's loss history with the Ohio History Connection before concluding a record does not exist.
- The 1790 federal census is effectively missing for Ohio as a practical matter — the territorial enumeration was incomplete and researchers should not assume it captured their ancestor.

## Research tips

- **The jurisdiction key rule:** For any event in 1790 Ohio, first determine whether it occurred in Washington County (1788, southeastern Ohio) or Hamilton County (1790, southwestern Ohio) — those were the only two organized counties. All of what is now Ohio that lay outside those county boundaries was unorganized territory with no county-level record-keeping. This distinction must be established before any repository search. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy," [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory))
- **Land records as the anchor:** Because no vital records or census exist for 1790 Ohio, land records and military bounty land warrants are the primary evidence of presence. Start with the BLM GLO website and the FamilySearch "Ohio, Land Records, 1787-1840" collection before any other record type.
- **Three land districts — three repositories:** Know which land district your ancestor's tract fell in before searching land records. Virginia Military District → Virginia State Library. Connecticut Western Reserve → Western Reserve Historical Society. Federal/U.S. Military District → BLM GLO. A search in the wrong repository will find nothing. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Ohio Genealogy — Land Records," [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records))
- **Revolutionary War pension files as biography:** If your ancestor served in the Revolutionary War, their pension file may contain the most detailed biographical record you will ever find — sworn testimony about birthplace, age, marriage, spouse's name, children, and residences. These are often the only source bridging the gap between 1775 and the 1800 census.
- **Work forward from the 1800 census:** Rather than expecting to find your ancestor in the 1790 period directly, identify them in the 1800 federal census, then work backward using tax records (1799-1803 Washington County volume on FamilySearch), land records, church records, and military files to establish their presence in 1790.
- **Ohio History Connection first for territorial records:** All records created under Northwest Territory authority before county organization, and many early county records that have been transferred out of county courthouses, are at the Ohio History Connection. Contact them before assuming a record does not exist.
- **Naming customs:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Ohio Naming Customs did not resolve in this survey. Be alert to patronymic elements in German and Scots-Irish families, and to the common practice of using a maternal grandmother's surname as a child's first name — a pattern that can create apparent surname variations in early records.
- **Church records are vital-record substitutes:** Since Ohio had no civil birth, marriage, or death registration in 1790, a church baptism record is the only dated birth evidence that will exist for children born that year. Search the FamilySearch "Ohio, Church Records, 1787-1950" collection and contact denominational archives directly.

---

Ohio in 1790 was part of the Northwest Territory — the future state did not exist yet, and the two organized counties (Washington, formed 1788, and Hamilton, formed 1790) were the only places where any American civil record-keeping occurred. For most of Ohio's territory in 1790, there simply was no county government and no official record-creation. The records that do survive come primarily from land grants (especially Revolutionary War bounty warrants, which are held in three separate repositories depending on which land district applies), from church baptism and marriage registers kept by circuit-riding ministers, and from county court minute books at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus. There is no civil birth, marriage, or death registration for 1790 Ohio, and the 1790 federal census did not effectively capture the Ohio territory. The most important warning is that which repository holds a given land record depends entirely on where in Ohio the land was located — Virginia Military District, Connecticut Western Reserve, or federal lands each route to a different archive.

The next step is to identify which county (Washington or Hamilton) or land district your specific ancestor was in, then build a targeted research plan focused on land records, military pension files, church registers, and the earliest available tax and census records from 1799-1803.

output.text_response:
Here is the locality-guide's response:

---

California for the Gold Rush years (roughly 1848 to 1865) has a rich but uneven record landscape. The state skipped the territorial phase and jumped directly to statehood in 1850, so U.S. county records begin that year. Before that, records are in Spanish and Latin from the Mexican and Mission-era systems. The most important single tool for placing a Gold Rush migrant is the **1852 California State Census**, which is 88% name-indexed on FamilySearch and fills the gap left by the partially destroyed 1850 federal census. Four major FamilySearch collections exist for the period — county births, county marriages, Great Registers (voter registration from 1866), and Mission Records — but **death records for the Gold Rush years are a serious gap** since statewide death registration did not function until 1905. The 1906 San Francisco earthquake destroyed the city's pre-earthquake vital records and court files entirely; anyone who passed through the city has a documentation hole there. Mining claim registers and port arrival registers are digitized but must be browsed image by image with no name search. For overland arrivals, manuscript diaries and company rosters at the **Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley** are the main resource and require an in-person visit. **Foreign Miners' Tax records** are an overlooked source for immigrant miners of any nationality and sit in county archives, largely undigitized.

Once you identify which county or mining district your ancestor was in, a county-level locality survey (for example, El Dorado, Placer, or Tuolumne County) would sharpen the repository list considerably before building a research plan.

quirks: The 1906 San Francisco Earthquake and Fire destroyed most pre-earthquake San Francisco vital records, naturalization files, and city court records — this is the single largest record loss for California genealogy.

The 1850 federal census was partially destroyed for California — some county returns are missing. The 1852 California State Census (FamilySearch imageGroupNumber 006601001, 88% indexed, full-text searchable) partially compensates and should be searched first.

California counties were created and subdivided rapidly through the 1850s. Confirm which county a given mining district fell under at the precise research date before selecting which courthouse to search.
Pre-1848 California records follow the Mexican/Spanish chain — Mission Records and diocesan records in Latin and Spanish — not U.S. county records, which begin only in 1850.

Foreign Miners' Tax records (1850, 1852) document non-citizen miners by name and nationality and are held at county archives; they are not comprehensively digitized and are especially important for Chinese, Mexican, Chilean, and French miners.
Pre-1906 naturalization files could be filed in any court of record at county level; a miner who moved between counties may have naturalized in a different county than where he mined.
Miners moved frequently between camps. Search neighboring goldfield counties (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Amador, Calaveras, Tuolumne) alongside the primary county of interest.

San Francisco Mining Claim Registers 1849-1855 (imageGroupNumber 006601002) and Sacramento Port Arrival Registers 1849-1858 (imageGroupNumber 006601003) are digitized but 0% indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only.

The Great Registers collection (1866-1910) begins after the Gold Rush peak but records a man's age, birthplace, occupation, and physical description — useful for tracing a miner who remained in California.
Overland trail arrivals left no single manifest record; manuscript diaries and company rosters at the Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) are the primary source for this large population.
