# Locality Guide: Louisiana (French Colonial Period, 1700–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** French Louisiana (La Louisiane) was claimed by France in 1682; New Orleans founded 1718. France ceded the western portion to Spain by the Treaty of Fontainebleau in 1762; the eastern portion went to Britain. Spain administered the western colony until secretly retroceding it to France in 1800, after which the Louisiana Purchase transferred the territory to the United States in 1803. (Wikipedia: [French Louisiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Louisiana))
- **Administrative center:** New Orleans (French colonial capital from 1718)
- **Parent jurisdictions:** New France (French Crown) 1699–1762; Spanish Louisiana 1769–1800; briefly French again 1800–1803
- **Population during period:** Population data from FamilySearch tools was not returned for this period. Colonial-era census rolls exist in French and Spanish archives (see Repositories below).
- **Economy:** Fur trade, indigo and tobacco cultivation, rice, later sugar; trade along the Mississippi River
- **Ethnic composition:** French settlers (including Canadians and Acadians), Spanish administrators from 1769, German Coast settlers, Afro-Louisianan (enslaved and free), Native nations, and later Anglo-American arrivals
- **Religious denominations:** The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized church under both French and Spanish rule. The Code Noir required Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons. The Archdiocese of New Orleans traces its institutional roots to this period.
- **Key historical events:** French colonization 1699; founding of New Orleans 1718; Natchez Massacre 1729; Seven Years' War; Treaty of Fontainebleau 1762 (French-to-Spanish transfer); Louisiana Purchase 1803

## Boundary changes

The 1700s saw significant jurisdictional layering with direct consequences for where records were created and are now held:

- **1699–1762 (French):** Records created under French civil and church authority. The Superior Council (Conseil Superieur) handled notarial, legal, and land matters. The Catholic parish was the unit of vital record-keeping.
- **1762–1769:** Nominal Spanish possession; French colonial administration continued in practice.
- **1769–1800 (Spanish):** Spanish replaced French civil administration. Cabildo (town council) replaced the Superior Council. Records shift from French to Spanish language. Notarial and church records continue but under Spanish forms.
- **1800–1803 (brief French, then U.S.):** Louisiana Purchase 1803. Records transition to U.S. territorial administration.

When researching any individual in this territory, you must determine which regime governed at the event date — French, Spanish, or transitional — because the language, legal form, and responsible archive differ.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

There was no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in French colonial Louisiana in the modern sense. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a Louisiana-specific vital records page. The Catholic Church performed all vital record functions during this period.

- **Pre-statehood:** No government-mandated civil vital registration existed during the French or Spanish colonial periods. Catholic parish sacramental registers are the primary and often only source.
- **What exists in church registers:** Baptisms (births), marriages, and burials from 1720 at St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans. A FamilySearch-confirmed collection, "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (Collection ID 1612905), covers this period and contains approximately 987,654 records with approximately 493,827 images at [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905).
- **Gaps:** Records before 1718 are sparse or nonexistent. Rural parishes outside New Orleans may have gaps throughout the period.
- **Language:** Records in this period are in French (1699–1769) and Spanish (1769–1803). Researchers must be able to read both, or work with translations.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Catholic only (legally mandated under French and Spanish rule)
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including of enslaved persons under the Code Noir), marriages, burials, and confirmations. The Code Noir requirement that enslaved people be baptized means Catholic registers document Afro-Louisianan families as well as free settlers.
- **Where held:** St. Louis Cathedral Archives (New Orleans); the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives; the Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans); and on FamilySearch microfilm.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" (Collection ID 1612905) — see above.
- **Language:** French and Spanish. These registers must be browsed in the original language.
- **Digitization level:** The FamilySearch volume search returned 2 digitized volumes for this period, both with 0% name-indexing and not full-text searchable. They must be browsed image-by-image.
  - Volume 004330991: 264 images, Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans, covering Orleans Parish, 1720–1803 (in French and Spanish)
  - Volume 004330992: 149 images, French colonial notarial acts (Superior Council records), covering Louisiana, 1699–1769 (in French and Spanish)
  - Both are browse-only — no name search is possible in these digitized images.

### Census records

- **Colonial census rolls:** France and Spain conducted periodic population counts of the colony. These are not federal censuses. The French colonial census rolls are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) in Aix-en-Provence, France, per the wiki_search result at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records).
- **U.S. federal census:** The first federal census applicable to U.S. Louisiana is 1810 (after the Purchase). The 1790 and 1800 censuses do not cover the territory.
- **Access:** Colonial census rolls are primarily physical or partially digitized at ANOM; no indexed FamilySearch collection for them was returned in this survey.

### Probate and court records (Superior Council / Cabildo)

- **Types:** Estate inventories, wills, contracts, court proceedings, land concession records. Under French rule these were handled by the Superior Council (Conseil Superieur). Under Spanish rule, the Cabildo.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984" (Collection ID 2078341), approximately 456,789 records with approximately 228,394 images, at [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341). The 1756 start date means the colonial-era probate records are included.
- **Digitized volume:** Volume 004330992 (see Church records above) covers French colonial notarial acts and Superior Council records, 1699–1769, in 149 browse-only images.
- **Where held (originals):** The Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) holds the Superior Council and Cabildo records. The wiki_search result at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records) states these have been partially digitized.
- **Language:** French (pre-1769), Spanish (1769–1803).

### Land records

- **Survey system:** French concession system (not the rectangular U.S. survey), using long-lot patterns along waterways. Spanish land grants followed similar forms.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under French rule, the Superior Council issued land concessions. Under Spanish rule, the Cabildo and Spanish governors. After 1803, the U.S. General Land Office reviewed and confirmed (or rejected) prior French and Spanish grants.
- **Types:** French concessions, Spanish grants, notarial acts of sale/transfer, American State Papers: Public Lands (which document confirmations of colonial-era grants), and records at the Louisiana State Land Office.
- **Notarial Archives:** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the 1730s onward — the wiki_search result at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants) describes it as the oldest continuous notarial office in North America.
- **Access:** Notarial Archives Research Center (New Orleans), in-person or online request; Louisiana State Land Office; BLM General Land Office records for post-1803 confirmations (online at glorecords.blm.gov); American State Papers available in print and on several online platforms.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** King William's War, Queen Anne's War, Natchez War (1729–1733), Seven Years' War (1754–1763), American Revolution (Louisiana under Spanish rule supported American forces)
- **Record types:** French colonial military service records; Spanish colonial muster rolls; pension records (very limited for this period)
- **Where held:** Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France holds French colonial military records. Spanish colonial military records are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain. NARA holds limited U.S.-period records only.
- **Access:** ANOM has a partial online catalog (anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr); physical visit or correspondence typically required for the records themselves.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (New Orleans, founded 1789 — Spanish period); earlier burials associated with church grounds.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has coverage for some Louisiana cemeteries, but 18th-century stones are rarely documented online.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, when they survive, are at the relevant church or diocesan archives.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The first Louisiana newspaper, Le Moniteur de la Louisiane, was not founded until 1794. No newspapers circulated during the French colonial period proper.
- **Where held:** Post-1794 papers are available at the Louisiana State University Libraries (Louisiana Digital Library) and other repositories.
- **Content value:** Not applicable for most of the 1700s; obituaries, marriage notices, and legal notices begin only in the final years of the Spanish period.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant arrivals:** French settlers arrived primarily from France, Canada (including the Acadian expulsion of 1755), and the Caribbean (Saint-Domingue). German settlers arrived along the German Coast from the 1720s.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists for the colonial period are fragmentary and are held primarily at ANOM. Naturalization as a U.S. concept does not apply until after 1803.
- **Where held:** ANOM (Aix-en-Provence) holds embarkation records and colonial correspondence that can document arrivals. The "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925" collection may document immigrant families' baptisms after arrival.
- **Content note:** Acadian exiles who arrived in Louisiana from 1765 onward are documented in specialized databases — the Council of Development of French in Louisiana (CODOFIL) and the Centre d'Etudes Acadiennes Anselme-Chiasson (Moncton, New Brunswick) hold relevant collections.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Colonial-era tax equivalents (capitation, labor obligations) were irregular and records are sparse.
- **Where held:** Any surviving tax-type records are within the Superior Council / Cabildo record series at the Louisiana Historical Center.
- **Substitute value:** Colonial census rolls and notarial records serve the role that tax lists play in other jurisdictions.

### Other record types

- **Notarial acts:** The New Orleans notarial records from the 1730s onward are among the richest sources for colonial Louisiana families. They document marriage contracts, property sales, manumissions, apprenticeships, and private agreements that never appear in vital or probate registers.
- **Code Noir compliance records:** Baptism of enslaved persons was legally required, making the Catholic sacramental registers a source for Afro-Louisianan genealogy in the colonial period.
- **Published local histories:** The Works Progress Administration (WPA) compiled significant Louisiana historical records in the 1930s–1940s, transcribing many colonial-era documents. Check WorldCat for WPA Louisiana collections.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (Collection 1612905, ~987,654 records, browse-only digitized volumes); Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 (Collection 2078341, ~456,789 records) | Free |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM) | French colonial administrative records, census rolls, military records, passenger records | Free catalog; physical/request for documents |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives | Notarial acts from 1730s onward | Online catalog; in-person research center |
| BLM General Land Office | Post-1803 land patent confirmations of colonial grants | Free online (glorecords.blm.gov) |
| FindAGrave | Some Louisiana cemetery records | Free |
| NARA | Post-1803 U.S.-period records only for this territory | Free online finding aids; some digitized |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 2 digitized volumes for Louisiana 1700–1803, which is the complete result set (totalResults: 2). Both are browse-only (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) and in French and Spanish. The FamilySearch collections_search returned 4 collections covering this place, but note that collection record counts as returned by the tool are not independently verified totals.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records, Cabildo records, partially digitized colonial documents | In-person; contact (504) 568-6968 |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Sacramental registers, diocesan correspondence | In-person/appointment |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial administrative correspondence, census rolls, military records, passenger lists | In-person; online catalog at anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial Louisiana records, 1769–1803 | In-person; PARES online portal (pares.mcu.es) |
| Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) | Post-1803 records; some Spanish-period materials | In-person; online finding aids |
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | Notarial acts from 1730s; oldest continuous notarial archive in North America | In-person; online index |

## Records NOT online

The following record types exist for French colonial Louisiana but are not available in any indexed online database:

- French colonial census rolls (at ANOM — no indexed FamilySearch collection returned)
- Spanish colonial muster rolls and military records (at Archivo General de Indias)
- Most Superior Council and Cabildo records outside the two browse-only FamilySearch volumes
- Pre-1794 newspapers (none existed)
- Colonial-period naturalization records (inapplicable under French/Spanish law; the U.S. naturalization framework postdates this period)
- Acadian arrival records (held at CODOFIL and Centre d'Etudes Acadiennes)

## Known record losses

- Some colonial-era records were lost or damaged during transitions between French, Spanish, and U.S. administration.
- The 1788 and 1794 New Orleans fires destroyed portions of the city; some church and notarial records from those years were affected.
- Hurricane and flood damage over the centuries has affected holdings at local repositories.
- **Substitute:** The notarial archives, which were maintained with great continuity, partially compensate for losses in other series.

## Research tips

- **The Catholic parish register is your birth, marriage, and death certificate.** No civil registration existed during this period. Start with FamilySearch Collection 1612905 ("Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925") and expect to browse images in French or Spanish without a name index, as both digitized colonial volumes (004330991 and 004330992) are 0% indexed. ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))
- **Know which regime governed at the event date.** French (1699–1769): records in French, filed with Superior Council and Catholic parishes. Spanish (1769–1803): records shift to Spanish, filed with the Cabildo and same Catholic parishes. Both regimes used the same parishes but different civil record-keeping structures. This changes which archive and which language applies.
- **The notarial archives are indispensable.** The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds marriage contracts, property transfers, manumissions, and private agreements from the 1730s onward — often naming relatives, witnesses, and associates not found in church registers. ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))
- **Research reaches across the Atlantic.** For French-period families, ANOM in Aix-en-Provence holds the administrative correspondence and census rolls of the colony. For Spanish-period families, the Archivo General de Indias in Seville holds colonial Louisiana records. A thorough search requires both American and European repositories.
- **The Code Noir requires baptism.** If you are researching enslaved or free Afro-Louisianan families, Catholic sacramental registers are legally mandated to include them. Look for baptismal entries for enslaved individuals, which name enslavers and sometimes godparents, providing relational data.
- **For Acadian ancestry:** The Acadian exiles who arrived in Louisiana from 1765 are a distinct population. Their earlier records (before the 1755 expulsion from Nova Scotia/Acadia) are in Maritime Canada, not Louisiana. Research must span both regions.
- **Long-lot land system:** French colonial land grants ran in long narrow strips perpendicular to waterways, not the rectangular U.S. township-and-range system. American State Papers: Public Lands documents the U.S. government's confirmation (or rejection) of French and Spanish grants after 1803 — these records name grantees and often describe the history of the claim, providing biographical detail.
- **Language:** Records are in French (1699–1769) and Spanish (1769–1803), with occasional Latin in sacramental contexts. Plan for translation assistance or paleographic training in colonial French and Spanish script.

---

French colonial Louisiana in the 1700s left a rich but challenging record landscape. The Catholic Church kept the only vital records that survive — baptisms, marriages, and burials in French and Spanish — while the Superior Council and later the Spanish Cabildo handled land, notarial, and court matters. Most of these records must be read in the original language and browsed image by image; no name-indexed online database covers the bulk of the colonial period. The main archives are split between New Orleans (Louisiana Historical Center, Notarial Archives, Archdiocese), France (ANOM in Aix-en-Provence), and Spain (Archivo General de Indias in Seville), so serious research requires reaching all three countries.

If you want to move forward, the next step is to narrow to a specific parish or family so a targeted research plan can map which of these record series to work through in sequence.

output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide returned by the research agent:

---

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (Late 1800s, c. 1850–1910)

**Surveyed counties:** Schuylkill (core), with parallel notes for Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Columbia, and Northumberland.

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Core coal counties:** Schuylkill (1811), Luzerne (1786), Carbon (1843), Lackawanna (1878), Northumberland, Columbia
- **County seats:** Pottsville (Schuylkill), Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne), Scranton (Lackawanna), Jim Thorpe / Mauch Chunk (Carbon)
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated; mining companies kept employment cards, pay ledgers, and accident reports
- **Ethnic communities:** Irish and Welsh (1820s–1870s), then Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian, and Ukrainian immigrants — each forming their own church congregations with records in multiple languages

---

## Key Boundary Changes

- **Lackawanna County** split from Luzerne in **1878** — records for the Scranton/Carbondale area **before 1878** are filed under **Luzerne County**
- **Carbon County** formed in **1843** from Northampton and Monroe — records for the Jim Thorpe/Mauch Chunk area before 1843 belong to those parent counties

---

## Record Types & Collections

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
Pennsylvania did **not** require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until **1906**. For the late 1800s, there are essentially no civil birth or death records for coal-county families. Church records are the primary substitute.

- **Marriage licenses** were kept at the county level from the colonial period onward
- *Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950* — FamilySearch (524,189 indexed records)
- *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* — FamilySearch (312,045 records)

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (Late 1800s, c. 1850–1910)

**Surveyed county:** Schuylkill County (the core of the anthracite region), with parallel notes for the other major coal counties: Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Columbia, and Northumberland.

---

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Core coal counties:** Schuylkill (formed 1811), Luzerne (formed 1786), Carbon (formed 1843 from Northampton and Monroe), Lackawanna (formed 1878 from Luzerne), Northumberland, Columbia
- **Administrative centers:** Pottsville (Schuylkill), Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne), Scranton (Lackawanna), Jim Thorpe / Mauch Chunk (Carbon)
- **Parent state:** Pennsylvania
- **Population:** No population figures were returned by the place tool for this survey period. The Wikipedia Coal Region article confirms that coal development from the 1820s through 1870s drew large and sustained immigration.
- **Economy:** Anthracite coal mining dominated. Mining companies maintained employment cards, pay ledgers, and accident reports. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds Mine Inspector reports from 1870. (Source: Wikipedia, [Coal Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region))
- **Ethnic composition:** Irish, Welsh, German (from the 1820s–1870s); later waves from Poland, Lithuania, Slovakia, Italy, and Ukraine. Each group generally formed its own church congregation, which means records exist in multiple languages and across many denominations.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic, Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Episcopalian, Lutheran, Reformed, Greek Catholic, Ukrainian Catholic, Baptist, Presbyterian, and numerous ethnic-language congregations
- **Key historical events:** Expansion of railroads (1840s–1870s) opened new collieries; the Molly Maguires trials (1876–1877) in Schuylkill County generated extensive court records; major mine disasters (Avondale, 1869; others) produced coroner inquests and newspaper coverage

---

## Boundary changes

- **Lackawanna County** was formed in 1878 from the northern portion of Luzerne County. Any records for the Scranton/Carbondale area before 1878 — including deeds, probate filings, marriage licenses, and court cases — were filed under Luzerne County. Search Luzerne first for ancestors in that area before 1878.
- **Carbon County** was formed in 1843 from Northampton and Monroe counties. Records before 1843 for the Mauch Chunk / Jim Thorpe area belong to those parent counties.
- **Schuylkill County** boundaries have been stable since its 1811 formation; Pottsville records go back to county founding.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require **statewide** civil registration of births and deaths until **1906**. Before that date, no statewide system covered the coal region. Philadelphia County began local registration in 1860 and Allegheny County in 1870 — but the coal counties are not among those early-adopting counties. For the late 1800s, there is effectively no civil birth or death record for most coal-region families. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))
- **Marriage records:** Marriage licenses were kept at the **county** level from the colonial period onward. County-level marriage records survive from county formation dates.
- **What exists online:**
  - "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950" — FamilySearch collection 1921317; 524,189 indexed records, 312,045 images. Covers the tail end of the target period and beyond.
  - "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950" — FamilySearch collection 1571957; 312,045 indexed records, 156,023 images.
  - "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900" — FamilySearch collection 1502909; 198,765 indexed records, index only (no images).
  - "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968" — FamilySearch collection 2255317; 4,218,763 indexed records with images. Begins just after the close of the late-1800s target window; valuable for family members who survived into the early 1900s.
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths for the 1850–1905 period have essentially no civil registration for these counties. Church records are the primary substitute.

### Church records

This is the most important source category for the coal region in the late 1800s, because church registration predates any civil system.

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Irish, Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, Italian, Ukrainian parishes — each kept separate registers); Welsh Calvinist Methodist; Welsh Congregational; Episcopal; German Lutheran; German Reformed; Ukrainian Greek Catholic; Byzantine Catholic; Baptist; Presbyterian. Many immigrant parishes kept records in the language of the congregation (Welsh, Polish, Slovak, German, Lithuanian, Ukrainian).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations (a separate dated event, often years after baptism — important for establishing an approximate birth year).
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records" — collection SYNTH-PA-CHURCH; 1,245,830 indexed records, 607,220 images, covering 1708–1985. This is the largest single indexed collection for the region.
- **Where held:** Parish originals remain at local churches or have been transferred to diocesan archives. Catholic records for the coal region fall under the Diocese of Allentown (for Schuylkill and Carbon) and the Diocese of Scranton (for Luzerne, Lackawanna). FamilySearch has microfilmed many parish registers.
- **Language warning:** Polish, Slovak, Ukrainian, and Welsh records are not in English. Latin appears in Catholic sacramental registers regardless of the parish's ethnic character.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** Decennial censuses 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910 cover the coal counties. The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed by fire and water damage in 1921 — it is a known gap for the whole country.
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 censuses include mortality schedules naming individuals who died in the year preceding the census — a critical substitute for missing civil death records in this period.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not take statewide intercensal censuses. The 1890 gap is not compensated by a state enumeration for these counties.
- **Access:** Federal census records 1850–1880 and 1900–1910 are fully indexed and searchable on both FamilySearch (free) and Ancestry (subscription). The [U.S. Federal Census Collection on Ancestry](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) covers all surviving years.

### Probate and court records

- **Probate types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions — held at the county Register of Wills from each county's formation date.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994" — collection 1999196; 3,200,560 images. **This collection has 0 indexed records** — it is **browse-only** and must be navigated image by image without a name index. Note that it is a significant repository nonetheless.
- **Court records:** The Molly Maguires trials (Schuylkill County, 1876–1877) produced an extensive court record. Naturalizations before 1906 could be filed in any court of record — Court of Common Pleas, Orphans' Court, or Quarter Sessions — at the county level.
- **Where held:** County courthouse for originals; FamilySearch images for browsing.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land was distributed by the colonial proprietors and then the Commonwealth, not the federal government).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania State Land Office in Harrisburg holds warrant, survey, and patent records going back to William Penn's original grants (1681). County deeds begin at each county's formation date and are held at the county Recorder of Deeds. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))
- **Types:** Warrants, surveys, patents, deeds, mortgages, tax assessment lists.
- **Tax records** (assessment lists, tax duplicates) survive in some Pennsylvania counties from the 1690s and serve as census substitutes before 1790 and between censuses. They are held at county archives or the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Where held:** County Recorder of Deeds for deeds; Pennsylvania State Archives for Land Office records.

### Occupational and mine records (coal-region specific)

This is the record category most distinctive to the coal towns and often overlooked in standard genealogical surveys.

- **Mine Worker Employment Cards (Schuylkill County, 1870–1900):** FamilySearch has digitized one volume (imageGroupNumber 002240015; 410 images; 95% name-indexed; also full-text searchable). This is the most accessible occupational record in the current tool results.
- **Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne County, 1870–1895):** FamilySearch volume 002240016; 287 images; **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only.**
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna County, 1878–1900):** FamilySearch volume 002240017; 199 images; **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — browse-only.**
- **Pennsylvania Mine Inspector Reports (from 1870):** Held at the Pennsylvania State Archives in Harrisburg. These annual reports name accident victims and sometimes list colliery workforce. (Source: Wikipedia, [Coal Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region))
- **Coverage note:** `volume_search` returned 23 total digitized volumes for this place and period but only the first page (3 volumes) was retrieved due to pagination. The 20 additional volumes were not examined in this survey. The next page token is available; ask for a follow-up survey to review them.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) is the dominant conflict for men born in the coal region during the 1830s–1840s; the Spanish-American War (1898) affected the next generation.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at the National Archives (NARA) in Washington, D.C., and searchable on [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) (subscription). Civil War draft registrations (1863) are also at NARA.
- **State records:** Pennsylvania adjutant general records at the Pennsylvania State Archives include regimental histories and muster rolls.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Numerous ethnic and denominational cemeteries in each coal town, often attached to a specific church (Polish Catholic, Welsh Methodist, Ukrainian Greek Catholic, etc.).
- **Online coverage:** [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) has broad coverage of coal-region cemeteries. BillionGraves also indexes headstone photographs.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers are held at individual churches or cemeteries. Not systematically digitized outside of Find A Grave and BillionGraves.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The coal region had an active press. The Miners' Journal (Pottsville, Schuylkill County) began publication in 1825 and is one of the oldest continuously published newspapers in the region. Scranton and Wilkes-Barre also had competing dailies.
- **Where held:** [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) (subscription) holds digitized historical newspaper runs. The State Library of Pennsylvania holds microfilm collections. Local public libraries (Pottsville Free Public Library, Osterhout Free Library in Wilkes-Barre) hold local microfilm runs.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, mine accident reports, legal notices, union organizing coverage, and Molly Maguires trial reporting are all genealogically significant.

### Immigration and naturalization records

The coal region received waves of immigrants throughout the late 1800s. Immigration records are often the key to tracing families back to their home village.

- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia and New York (Castle Garden through 1890, Ellis Island from 1892) are the primary arrival ports for coal-region immigrants.
- **Passenger lists:** Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry. For pre-1906 arrivals, manifest detail varies — earlier lists give little information, while post-1895 lists include last residence, contact person in destination country, and destination address in the U.S.
- **Naturalization:** Before 1906, naturalization could occur in any court of record. Coal-region naturalizations are scattered across the Court of Common Pleas in each county. After September 27, 1906, all naturalizations went through federal courts and copies to the Bureau of Immigration. Search both county court records and the NARA federal naturalization index.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest — not just the head of household — for all family members, including children as young as newborns.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Property tax (assessment lists), poll tax, personal property tax — held at each county seat.
- **Date range:** Pennsylvania tax assessment lists survive in some counties from the late colonial period; for the coal counties, records typically begin at county formation.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for the lost 1890 census. A person appearing in 1880 and 1900 census records can often be traced through consecutive annual tax assessments in the intervening decade.
- **Where held:** County archives and the Pennsylvania State Archives. Many have not been digitized.

### Other record types

- **School records:** Individual school districts kept enrollment and attendance records; survival is uneven. Check local county historical society archives.
- **Mine union records:** The United Mine Workers of America (organized 1890) and its predecessor organizations kept membership records. These may survive in union archives or regional depositories.
- **Published county histories:** 19th-century county histories for Schuylkill, Luzerne, and Carbon counties list founding families and early settlers and sometimes contain biographical sketches of mine operators and community leaders. Check WorldCat for available volumes.

## Known record losses

Affects the entire country; no substitution exists except tax lists, city directories, and state enumerations (Pennsylvania took none). This is the most significant gap for the 1880–1900 research window.
- No major courthouse fires specifically documented in the tool results for the core coal counties. The Pennsylvania State Archives should be consulted for any local records-loss documentation.

---

## Research tips

- **No statewide birth/death registration before 1906:** For any vital event in the coal region before 1906, church records are the only source. Identify the specific church the family attended (which is tied to ethnicity and denomination) before searching broadly. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))
- **Lackawanna County split in 1878:** Records for the Scranton/Carbondale area before 1878 were filed under Luzerne County — search Luzerne County's deed, probate, and court records for ancestors in that area before that date. (Source: Wikipedia, [Coal Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region); confirmed by place_search result for Lackawanna County)
- **Carbon County split in 1843:** Records for the Jim Thorpe / Mauch Chunk area before 1843 are in Northampton and Monroe county records.
- **Ethnic church is the key jurisdictional unit:** The civil county does not tell you which parish kept an ancestor's baptism record. Welsh families went to Welsh Calvinist or Congregational churches; Irish to Roman Catholic; Polish/Slovak/Lithuanian to separate national Catholic parishes; Ukrainians to Greek Catholic or Ukrainian Catholic. Each had its own register, often in the heritage language.
- **Marriage licenses at the county level from the colonial period:** Even before statewide civil registration, marriage licenses survive at county courthouses. The indexed FamilySearch collections for PA marriages cover 1677 onward.
- **Mine occupational records are an underused source:** Employment cards (95% indexed for Schuylkill, 1870–1900), payroll ledgers, and accident reports name individuals who may not appear in other searchable sources. Browse-only volumes for Luzerne and Lackawanna require image-by-image review.
- **Mortality schedules as death-record substitutes:** The 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal census mortality schedules name individuals who died in the year before the census and include cause of death — the closest available substitute for civil death registration in those decades.
- **Naturalization records are scattered before 1906:** A pre-1906 declaration of intention or final naturalization papers could be filed in any court in any state — not necessarily in the county where the person lived at the time of the census. Search the county Court of Common Pleas records first, but do not stop there.
- **Surname spelling variation is extreme in this region:** Irish, Welsh, Polish, Slovak, and Ukrainian surnames were frequently anglicized, misspelled by clerks unfamiliar with the language, or recorded phonetically. Search broadly, use wildcard searches, and check variant spellings systematically.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania did not return place-specific content** in this survey run — all four wiki_place_page sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only a generic fallback page rather than Pennsylvania-specific guidance. The Pennsylvania Vital Records and Land Records information above comes from wiki_search results that did return substantive Pennsylvania-specific content. Pennsylvania coal-region families from the late 1800s left records across several distinct systems: church registers (because state civil registration of births and deaths did not begin until 1906), county marriage licenses, federal census records (with the 1890 gap), probate and deed records at each county courthouse, mine employment and accident records, naturalization papers scattered across county courts, and — for immigrants — passenger arrival lists. The next step, if you want to move from this overview to a targeted search strategy for a specific family, is to identify which county and which church congregation that family belonged to — that narrows the search to the right register and the right courthouse series.

## Massachusetts Early 1600s Puritan Settlements — Locality Guide

A locality entry has been saved to your project. Here's a summary of the key findings:

---

### Why This Era Is Uniquely Rich
Massachusetts is exceptional compared to most of North America in the 1600s: the colony mandated **town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths starting in 1639**, making it one of the earliest jurisdictions to require civil vital registration.

---

### Key Record Types & Repositories

**1. Town Vital Records (Post-1639)**
- Births, marriages, and deaths recorded at the town level.
- Transcribed into a published series covering **200+ towns**, partially searchable on **FamilySearch** (Collection 2061550).

**2. Congregational Church Records (From ~1630)**
- Often the earliest records for a family.
- A Suffolk County church volume on FamilySearch is full-text searchable (though not name-indexed).

**3. Great Migration Study Series**
- For any ancestor arriving **before 1643**, the *Great Migration* study series at **AmericanAncestors.org** (New England Historic Genealogical Society) is the field's authoritative starting point — highly detailed, thoroughly sourced.

**4. County Probate & Deed Records**
- Essential for reconstructing family relationships and property holdings.

---

### Critical Caveats

⚠️ **Plymouth Colony** was a completely separate legal jurisdiction from Massachusetts Bay **until 1691** — it has its own published records and must be searched independently.

⚠️ **King Philip's War (1675–1676)** destroyed the early town records of many frontier settlements.

---

### Recommended Next Step
Identify which specific **town** your ancestor lived in, then focus on:
1. That town's vital record volume
2. The local Congregational church register
3. County probate and deed records

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Massachusetts Bay Colony founded 1628; Plymouth Colony founded 1620; merged into Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691
- **Administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown; colonial charter
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fishing, timber, trade
- **Ethnic composition:** Primarily English Puritan settlers; small numbers of non-Puritan English, Dutch, indentured servants; Indigenous nations (Wampanoag, Massachusetts, Narragansett)
- **Religious denominations:** Congregational (established); small persecuted Quaker and Baptist communities
- **Key historical events:** Great Migration 1630-1640; King Philip's War 1675-1676; Salem Witch Trials 1692

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628-1691) were completely separate jurisdictions until 1691 merger.
- Maine was part of Massachusetts jurisdiction during this period.
- Counties established 1643: Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk (now-abolished), York (Maine).

## Available record types

### Vital records
- Town-level recording mandated 1639 by Massachusetts Bay Colony
- FamilySearch collection 2061550 (Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890)
- Published Tanner-Corbin 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series for 200+ towns
- Gaps: King Philip's War destroyed many frontier town records

### Church records
- Congregational meetings kept membership lists, baptisms, marriages, burials, disciplinary proceedings
- FamilySearch collection 1921657 (Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920)
- Volume 007612045: Suffolk Co. Congregational admissions/baptisms 1630-1700 — full-text searchable, not name-indexed
- Congregational Library & Archives, Boston holds originals

### Census records
- No federal census until 1790 — not applicable
- Freeman rolls (published) substitute for heads of household
- Tax lists and militia musters serve as census substitutes

### Probate and court records
- FamilySearch collection 1678901 (Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991)
- County probate courts from 1640s: Essex, Middlesex, Suffolk
- Plymouth Colony probate published in Shurtleff volumes
- Massachusetts General Court session records published (Shurtleff, 5 vols.)

### Land records
- State-land state; metes-and-bounds system
- Volume 007612044: town meeting and proprietors' records 1620-1698 (browse-only, 188 images)
- County Registries of Deeds from 1630s
- Massachusetts Archives holds colonial-era grants

### Military records
- Pequot War (1636-1637); King Philip's War (1675-1676)
- Militia lists and muster rolls at Massachusetts Archives
- No NARA federal records for pre-federal period

### Cemetery records
- Major colonial burial grounds: King's Chapel (1630), Copp's Hill (1659), Granary (1660), Salem, Ipswich
- FindAGrave coverage available
- Many 17th-century wooden markers have not survived

### Newspaper records
- No newspapers until 1690; Boston News-Letter began 1704 — outside target window
- Substitute: published town histories, Governor Winthrop's Journal

### Immigration records
- Great Migration study (NEHGS/AmericanAncestors.org) covers every known settler 1620-1643
- Ship lists fragmentary; Banks' 'Planters of the Commonwealth' is best compilation
- FamilySearch passenger list collection (1784312) covers 1820-1891 only — not applicable

### Tax records
- Town-level tax lists from early settlement
- Massachusetts Archives and published town histories
- Substitute for missing census years

## Repository guide

### Online
| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Town Vital Records 1620-1890; Church Records 1630-1920; Probate Records 1635-1991; 2 digitized volumes | Free |
| AmericanAncestors.org (NEHGS) | Great Migration study; NEHG Register; manuscript collections | Subscription |
| HathiTrust/Google Books | Published Plymouth Colony records; local histories | Free |
| FindAGrave | Colonial burial grounds | Free |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Colony records, court records, vital records from 1620s | In-person; some online |
| NEHGS, Boston | Great Migration manuscripts; NEHG Register | In-person/AmericanAncestors.org |
| Massachusetts Historical Society | Winthrop Journal; diaries; manuscripts | In-person; some digitized |
| Congregational Library & Archives | Church registers | In-person; some online |
| County Registries of Deeds | Deed books from 1630s | In-person; some via MassLandRecords.com |

## Records NOT online
- Most town meeting/proprietors' records beyond the 2 digitized FamilySearch volumes
- Congregational church registers outside Suffolk County not confirmed digitized
- County court of common pleas records outside published volumes
- Militia/muster rolls for King Philip's War

## Known record losses
- King Philip's War (1675-1676) destroyed town records for many frontier settlements
- Early 1630s-1640s church registers frequently never kept or lost

## Research tips
- Start with the Great Migration study (AmericanAncestors.org) for any ancestor arriving 1620-1643
- Distinguish Plymouth Colony from Massachusetts Bay Colony — entirely separate jurisdictions until 1691
- Town vital records are town-level (mandated 1639), not statewide
- Church membership rolls are genealogically critical — often the only dated record linking a person to a town
- Freeman rolls published and indexed — use as census substitute for heads of household
- Full-text search (not name search) required for volume 007612045
- Browse image-by-image for volume 007612044 (no index, no full-text)
- Calendar: Julian calendar used until 1752; double-year dates (e.g., 1671/72) before March 25
- Search neighboring colony records (Connecticut, Rhode Island, New Hampshire) for border families

output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide returned by the research agent:

---

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma (Land Run Era, 1889–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory created May 2, 1890 under the Organic Act, following the Land Run of April 22, 1889. Oklahoma achieved statehood November 16, 1907, merging Oklahoma Territory (western portion) with Indian Territory (eastern portion).
- **Administrative center:** Guthrie (territorial capital); Oklahoma City (state capital from 1910)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** U.S. federal government (as an organized territory); Indian Territory existed as a parallel jurisdiction covering eastern Oklahoma
- **Population:** The 1889 Land Run brought an estimated 50,000 settlers in a single day; by statehood the combined territories held several hundred thousand residents.
- **Ethnic composition:** Settlers came primarily from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, Arkansas, and the Midwest, with significant African American settlement (freedmen communities and all-Black towns). The Five Civilized Tribes occupied Indian Territory to the east.
- **Key events:** Land Run of April 22, 1889; creation of Oklahoma Territory 1890; subsequent land runs 1891–1895; Dawes Commission enrollment 1898–1914; statehood 1907.

---

## Boundary changes

Oklahoma Territory was created from the Unassigned Lands in 1890 and expanded through subsequent land openings. Before May 2, 1890, there was no formal territorial government. Indian Territory (eastern Oklahoma) operated under separate tribal governance until statehood. At statehood, county boundaries were drawn for both halves simultaneously.

**Critical dual-jurisdiction pattern:** A family in western Oklahoma generated territorial court and General Land Office records. A family in eastern Oklahoma generated tribal court records, BIA agency records, and Dawes Commission enrollment records — in completely different repositories.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Start date:** Statewide vital registration began **October 1908** (one year after statehood); compliance was poor until the 1930s.
- **What exists:** State birth and death records from October 1908 onward, held by the Oklahoma State Archives. For the **1889–1907 territorial period, no civil vital registration existed at any level.**
- **Exception — marriage:** County-level marriage registers begin at county formation (1890 onward). FamilySearch holds **Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995** (collection 2134789; 456,789 records).
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records, cemetery records, newspaper notices, census records, and homestead proof affidavits (which state ages and names of family members on the claim).

### Church Records

- **Denominations:** Baptist, Methodist Episcopal, Methodist Episcopal South, Catholic; mission churches had preceded the Land Run since the 1820s–1830s.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (collection 1654321; 123,456 records).
- **Physical holdings:** Oklahoma Conference of the United Methodist Church Archives; Diocese of Oklahoma City for Catholic records.

### Census Records

- **1890 federal census:** Almost entirely destroyed nationwide — but the **1890 Oklahoma Territory special census** is one of the few surviving fragments, held by the Oklahoma Historical Society.
- **1900 and 1910 federal censuses:** Available and cover both Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory as separate enumeration districts. Indexed and imaged on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Indian Territory censuses:** Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (FamilySearch collection 1987432; 567,890 records).
- **Dawes rolls:** Digitized on FamilySearch as a browse-only volume (imageGroupNumber 005221389; 176 images; 0% name-indexed — must be browsed page by page).
- **County tax rolls:** Exist from 1890s and document settlers between census enumerations; held at the Oklahoma Historical Society and county courthouses.

### Probate and Court Records

- **Territorial courts:** Oklahoma Territory had a federal district court structure (1890–1907). Records are at **NARA at Fort Worth** (Record Group 21) and the Oklahoma State Archives.
- **County probate:** From 1890 onward at county district courts; records at county courthouses.
- **Indian Territory courts:** Separate tribal court systems plus U.S. Court for the Indian Territory; records at NARA Fort Worth.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 declarations could be filed in any court of record; search territorial district courts at NARA Fort Worth.

### Land Records

- **Key record type for this era:** Homestead applications, final certificates, land patents, rejected applications. Each homestead file typically includes the original application, **proof of settlement with witnesses** (naming family members present on the claim), and the final patent.
- **Land offices:** Established at Guthrie and Kingfisher immediately after the 1889 Land Run; additional offices opened with subsequent runs.
- **Where held:** National Archives, Washington, D.C. (Record Group 49, General Land Office); partially indexed on FamilySearch; searchable at **glorecords.blm.gov** (free).
- **FamilySearch collections:** Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 (collection 1541872; 234,567 records); digitized homestead case files volume (imageGroupNumber 005221388; 402 images; 74% name-indexed).

### Military Records

- **Context:** Many Land Run settlers were Civil War veterans. The Spanish-American War (1898) also drew Oklahoma Territory men.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA Washington, D.C. **Civil War pension files** are particularly valuable — they document family composition, marriage dates, and addresses across decades.
- **Online:** Fold3.com (subscription).

### Cemetery Records

- Each Land Run town established cemeteries almost immediately; **FindAGrave** covers many Oklahoma cemeteries (free). Black townsite communities (Boley, Langston, Rentiesville, etc.) had their own cemeteries.

### Newspaper Records

- **Local papers:** Established within days of the 1889 Land Run (Guthrie Daily Leader, Oklahoma State Capital, etc.).
- **Online:**
  - **Gateway to Oklahoma History** (gateway.okhistory.org) — free access to digitized Oklahoma newspapers
  - **Newspapers.com** — subscription
  - Oklahoma Historical Society newspaper microfilm
- **Critical tip:** Homestead final proof notices were legally required to be published in a local newspaper. Searching territorial newspapers (1892–1898) can surface your ancestor's claim notice, naming themselves, their witnesses, and their land description.

### Dawes Commission Enrollment Files

- The fullest genealogical record for families with Five Civilized Tribes or Freedmen ancestry. Enrollment jackets contain birth dates, family relationships, and often photographs.
- **Where held:** National Archives at Fort Worth (originals); partially digitized on FamilySearch (browse-only, imageGroupNumber 005221389).

### Tax Records

- Personal property and real property tax rolls from 1890 onward at county level.
- **Substitute value:** Invaluable for filling the 1890–1900 gap; document presence in a county year by year.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society; county courthouses.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online

| Repository | Collections | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Early Land Records 1834–1907 (1541872); Indian Censuses & Rolls 1851–1959 (1987432); County Marriages 1890–1995 (2134789); Mission & Church Records 1820–1965 (1654321); homestead case files volume; Dawes enrollment jackets (browse-only) | Free |
| BLM GLO Records (glorecords.blm.gov) | Land patents and homestead files | Free |
| Gateway to Oklahoma History (gateway.okhistory.org) | Digitized Oklahoma territorial newspapers | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal censuses (1900, 1910); military records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records, pension files | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Digitized Oklahoma newspapers | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** (Oklahoma City) | 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census; land run claim files; town lot records; tax rolls; newspapers; county histories |
| **Oklahoma State Archives** (Oklahoma City) | State birth/death records from October 1908; territorial government records |
| **NARA at Fort Worth** | Territorial district court records (RG 21); Dawes Commission files; Bureau of Indian Affairs records (RG 75); U.S. Court for the Indian Territory records |
| **NARA Washington, D.C.** | General Land Office records (RG 49); homestead application files; military service and pension records |
| County courthouses | County marriage registers from 1890; deed records; county probate files |
| Oklahoma Conference of the United Methodist Church Archives | Methodist church registers |
| Diocese of Oklahoma City Archives | Catholic parish registers |

---

## Records NOT Online

- The 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census (physical at Oklahoma Historical Society; not fully digitized)
- County tax rolls (1890s–1900s) — largely physical at OHS and county courthouses
- Town lot records for territorial-era townsites — physical at OHS
- Most territorial court case files — physical at NARA Fort Worth or Oklahoma State Archives
- Many local church registers
- Individual tribal court records from Indian Territory

---

## Known Record Losses

The territorial period (1889–1907) is characterized by sparse record-keeping rather than destruction — the infrastructure was simply being built from scratch. However:

- The near-total destruction of the **1890 federal census nationwide** is the single biggest gap; the surviving 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census at OHS is therefore uniquely important.
- Individual county courthouse losses may exist at the local level — confirm with each courthouse before assuming a record is gone.
- Many early church registers were kept by itinerant ministers and were never deposited in any archive.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with homestead records, not vital records.** For 1889–1908, no civil birth or death registration existed. The homestead final proof affidavit — filed five years after the original claim — often names the settler's family, ages, and two witnesses. Search FamilySearch collection 1541872 and glorecords.blm.gov first.

2. **Search the newspaper for the homestead proof publication.** Legally required to be published near the land office, these notices name the claimant, witnesses, and legal land description. Use Gateway to Oklahoma History (free) for territorial newspapers.

3. **The 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census is unique.** It is one of the only windows into the 1889–1900 population. Contact the Oklahoma Historical Society directly for access.

4. **Trace the settler's departure state before searching Oklahoma.** Most families came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and Arkansas. The 1900 Oklahoma census shows birthplace of parents — use that to pivot to the departure state's records for origins, parents, and earlier vital events.

5. **Eastern vs. western Oklahoma — determine which territory first.** Western Oklahoma (Oklahoma Territory) = territorial courts + GLO records. Eastern Oklahoma (Indian Territory) = tribal courts + BIA records + Dawes Commission. These are in different record groups at NARA and require different search strategies.

6. **Dawes enrollment files are essential for Five Civilized Tribes and Freedmen ancestry.** Enrollment jackets contain family group information not found anywhere else. Even families with partial ancestry should check these rolls, as many filed applications who ultimately were not enrolled.

7. **Vital registration compliance was poor even after 1908.** A missing birth or death certificate before 1930 should not be taken as proof the event did not occur — seek church records, obituaries, and census records as corroboration.

8. **Civil War pension files document family composition.** Many Land Run settlers were Civil War veterans. Pension files contain marriage dates, names of children, and decades of correspondence — often more detailed than any vital record.

9. **County tax rolls substitute for census gaps.** Annual personal property and real property rolls survive from 1890 at the Oklahoma Historical Society and are among the few records documenting county-by-county presence during the 1890s.

---

**Bottom line for the Land Run era:** The most important record classes are (1) homestead files, (2) the 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census, (3) county marriage registers, and (4) territorial newspaper proof publications — all filling the gap left by the complete absence of civil vital registration before 1908. For families with Indian Territory connections, add the Dawes Commission enrollment jackets at NARA Fort Worth. The Oklahoma Historical Society and NARA Fort Worth are the two indispensable physical repositories for this period.

Marriage records are the exception: county-level marriage registers begin at county formation (1890 onward in Oklahoma Territory), and FamilySearch holds the collection "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995" (collection 2134789; 456,789 records, 228,394 images).
- **Where held:** State births/deaths from 1908: Oklahoma State Archives, Oklahoma City. County marriages from 1890: county courthouses; indexed + images on FamilySearch (collection 2134789).
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration for the territorial period (1889–1908). Compliance gaps persist through the 1920s even after registration began.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records, cemetery records, newspaper notices, census records, and homestead proof affidavits (which state ages and names of family members present on the claim).

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist Episcopal, Methodist Episcopal South, Catholic; mission churches of various denominations had served Indian Territory since the 1820s–1830s.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and confirmations. FamilySearch holds "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965" (collection 1654321; 123,456 records, 61,728 images) — this collection spans the mission era through the post-statehood period.
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Conference of the United Methodist Church Archives; Diocese of Oklahoma City for Catholic records; FamilySearch microfilm and the above collection for mission and early church registers. ([Oklahoma Vital Records — Repositories](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records#Repositories))
- **Language:** English. Mission-era records for Indian Territory may include records kept in the Cherokee syllabary or other tribal writing systems.
- **Coverage note:** Church records begin sporadically in 1889 as denominations established congregations in the new towns. ([Oklahoma Territorial Records — Territorial Courts and Early Settlement](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts))

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The 1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed nationwide — but uniquely, the 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census is one of the few surviving fragments, held by the Oklahoma Historical Society. The 1900 and 1910 federal censuses are available and cover both Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory as separate enumeration districts. The 1880 federal census covers the region under Kansas and other surrounding states (settlers had not yet arrived). ([Oklahoma Vital Records — Registration History](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records#Registration_History))
- **Indian Territory censuses:** The "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959" collection on FamilySearch (collection 1987432; 567,890 records, 283,945 images) documents tribal members across the entire period and is essential for any family with Native American or Freedmen ancestry in Indian Territory.
- **Tribal/Dawes rolls:** The Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (1898–1910) are digitized on FamilySearch as a browse-only volume (imageGroupNumber 005221389; 176 images; 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). These must be browsed image by image. The Dawes rolls formally enrolled members of the Five Civilized Tribes and their Freedmen for purposes of allotment.
- **Tax rolls:** County tax rolls from the 1890s exist and can document settlers in the years between census enumerations. Held at the Oklahoma Historical Society and county courthouses.
- **Access:** 1900 and 1910 federal censuses are indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census and tax rolls are physical/microfilm at the Oklahoma Historical Society.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions, civil suits, criminal cases, and — critically for this period — naturalizations.
- **Territorial courts:** Oklahoma Territory had a federal district court structure (1890–1907). Territorial court records including probate and naturalization records are held at the National Archives at Fort Worth (Record Group 21) and the Oklahoma State Archives. ([Oklahoma Territorial Records — Territorial Courts and Early Settlement](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts))
- **County probate:** From 1890 onward, county district courts handled probate at the county level. Records are at county courthouses.
- **Indian Territory courts:** Separate tribal court systems operated in Indian Territory; federal courts (U.S. Court for the Indian Territory) also held jurisdiction. These records are at NARA at Fort Worth.
- **Naturalization note:** Pre-1906 naturalization declarations could be filed in any court of record. For territorial Oklahoma, this means territorial district courts. Search NARA at Fort Worth.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Rectangular survey (federal public domain, township-range-section). Oklahoma is a federal-land state — land grants originate with the federal government, not the state.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The General Land Office (now Bureau of Land Management) administered homestead applications. Land offices were established at Guthrie and Kingfisher immediately after the 1889 Land Run; additional offices opened as subsequent runs occurred. ([Oklahoma Land Records — Land Run and Homestead Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run))
- **Types:** Homestead applications, final certificates, land patents, rejected applications. Each homestead file typically includes the original application, proof of settlement with witnesses (naming family members present on the claim), and the final patent. Rejected applications also survive and contain family details.
- **Where held:** National Archives, Washington, D.C. (Record Group 49, General Land Office). Partially indexed on FamilySearch and searchable at BLM GLO Records website (glorecords.blm.gov). FamilySearch also holds the collection "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907" (collection 1541872; 234,567 records, 117,283 images). A digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 005221388; 402 images; 74% name-indexed, not full-text searchable) covers land-entry case files / homestead final proofs, 1889–1907. ([Oklahoma Land Records — Land Run and Homestead Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run))
- **Homestead final proof affidavits** are particularly valuable: they state the settler's name, age, family composition, date of entry, and names of two witnesses who can themselves become research subjects.
- **Town lots:** Oklahoma Territory towns (Guthrie, Kingfisher, Norman, etc.) were established immediately after the Land Run; town lot records are held by the Oklahoma Historical Society.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The Spanish-American War (1898) drew Oklahoma Territory men; some settlers were Civil War veterans. The Indian Wars generated pension files for some settlers and tribal members.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files at NARA Washington, D.C.; Civil War pension files are particularly valuable because they document family composition, marriage dates, and addresses decades after the war. Draft registrations (WWI) begin 1917, outside the core period but document the same generation.
- **Where held:** NARA; Fold3.com (subscription) for many military records online.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Each of the Land Run towns established cemeteries almost immediately; many are documented on FindAGrave (findagrave.com, free). The Black townsite communities (Boley, Langston, Rentiesville, etc.) had their own cemeteries.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave covers many Oklahoma cemeteries.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records, where they survive, are at local cemeteries or the Oklahoma Historical Society.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** Newspapers were established within days of the 1889 Land Run — the Guthrie Daily Leader and Oklahoma State Capital began in 1889. Newspapers proliferated rapidly with each new town.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription) holds digitized Oklahoma newspapers. The Oklahoma Historical Society holds extensive newspaper microfilm. The Gateway to Oklahoma History (gateway.okhistory.org) provides free access to digitized Oklahoma newspapers.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, homestead proof publication notices (legally required — settlers published notice in a local paper before submitting final proof, naming themselves, their witnesses, and their claim), marriage notices, legal filings.
- **Critical research tip:** Homestead final proof notice had to be published in a newspaper near the land office — searching local newspapers of 1892–1898 can surface your ancestor's claim five years after they filed.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Context:** Land Run settlers were internal migrants, not international immigrants, for the most part. However, many had immigrant parents: tracing the family back to the departure state (Kansas, Texas, Missouri, Arkansas) is necessary before reaching any port-of-entry record.
- **Record types:** For ancestors who were themselves foreign-born, naturalization records in territorial courts (NARA at Fort Worth) are the primary in-Oklahoma record. Passenger arrival records for their original immigration are at NARA and searchable on Ancestry/FamilySearch.
- **African American settlers:** Many freedmen communities in Oklahoma were formed by people who had been enslaved in Indian Territory (Freedmen of the Five Tribes) or who migrated from Southern states. The Dawes rolls and freedmen enrollment files are the primary records for Freedmen of the Five Tribes.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Personal property and real property tax rolls at county level from 1890 onward.
- **Date range:** From county formation (1890 in Oklahoma Territory).
- **Where held:** Oklahoma Historical Society holds many territorial-era tax rolls; county courthouses hold later records.
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls are invaluable for the 1890s, filling the gap between the largely-destroyed 1890 census and the 1900 census. They document presence in a county year by year.

### Other record types

- **Dawes Commission enrollment files:** The fullest genealogical record for families with Five Civilized Tribes or Freedmen ancestry. Enrollment jackets contain birth dates, family relationships, and often photographs. National Archives at Fort Worth holds the originals; partially digitized on FamilySearch (browse-only, imageGroupNumber 005221389).
- **Indian agency records:** Federal agents maintained records of Native American communities in Indian Territory from the 1830s. Record Group 75 (Bureau of Indian Affairs) at NARA.
- **Town and county histories:** Many Oklahoma counties published histories in the 1910s–1920s, shortly after statehood, often containing biographical sketches of pioneer families and transcriptions of early records. The Oklahoma Historical Society library holds many.
- **School records:** Territorial schools were established quickly; the Five Civilized Tribes maintained their own school systems in Indian Territory, with records at the Oklahoma Historical Society.
- **Oklahoma Historical Society published indexes:** The OHS has published indexes to territorial-era records not yet digitized online.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| FamilySearch | Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 (collection 1541872; 234,567 records); Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (collection 1987432; 567,890 records); Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995 (collection 2134789; 456,789 records); Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 (collection 1654321; 123,456 records); digitized homestead case files volume (74% indexed); Dawes enrollment jackets (browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1900, 1910 for Oklahoma Territory / Indian Territory); military records | Subscription |
| BLM GLO Records | Land patents and homestead files (glorecords.blm.gov) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Digitized Oklahoma newspapers (territorial-era included) | Subscription |
| Gateway to Oklahoma History | Digitized Oklahoma newspapers (gateway.okhistory.org) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records, pension files | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** volume_search returned a total of 2 digitized volumes matching Oklahoma for this period; both are detailed above. This appears to be the complete result set (no nextPageToken returned). The collections_search returned 4 collections, all detailed above. These represent what is indexed/digitized on FamilySearch; a large body of additional microfilm exists and is catalogued separately.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
