| Oklahoma Historical Society (Oklahoma City) | 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census; land run claim files; town lot records; tax rolls; newspapers; county histories; territorial-era county records | In-person; some records available by mail/online request |
| Oklahoma State Archives (Oklahoma City) | State birth and death records from October 1908; territorial government records | In-person; vital records by mail request |
| National Archives at Fort Worth (NARA) | Territorial district court records (RG 21); Dawes Commission files; Bureau of Indian Affairs records (RG 75); U.S. Court for the Indian Territory records | In-person; some records on microfilm or digitized |
| NARA Washington, D.C. | General Land Office records (RG 49); homestead application files; military service and pension records | In-person; some records at glorecords.blm.gov or Fold3 |
| County courthouses | County marriage registers from 1890; deed records; county probate files | In-person or mail; many marriages indexed on FamilySearch |
| Oklahoma Conference of the United Methodist Church Archives | Methodist Episcopal and ME South church registers | Contact the archive directly |
| Diocese of Oklahoma City Archives | Catholic parish registers | Contact the archive directly |

---

## Records NOT online

- The 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census (physical at Oklahoma Historical Society; not fully digitized)
- County-level tax rolls (1890s–1900s) — largely physical at OHS and county courthouses
- Town lot records for territorial-era townsites — physical at OHS
- Most territorial court case files beyond the digitized volume — physical at NARA Fort Worth or Oklahoma State Archives
- Many local church registers not captured in the FamilySearch mission/church collection
- Sexton and burial registers for individual cemeteries
- Individual tribal court records from Indian Territory (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, Seminole courts)

---

## Known record losses

The territorial period (1889–1907) is generally characterized by sparse record-keeping rather than destruction: record-keeping infrastructure was simply being built from scratch. No major statewide courthouse fire is documented for this period in the tool results. However:

- The near-total destruction of the 1890 federal census nationwide means researchers have no national enumeration for 1889–1900 — the surviving 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census at OHS is therefore uniquely important.
- Individual county courthouse losses may exist at the local level; researchers should confirm with each county courthouse before assuming a record does not exist.
- Many early church registers were kept by itinerant ministers and were never deposited in any archive.

---

## Research tips

- **Start with homestead records, not vital records.** For the 1889–1908 period, no civil birth or death registration existed at any level. The homestead final proof affidavit — filed five years after the original claim — is often the first document that names the settler's family, ages, and witnesses. Search FamilySearch collection 1541872 and glorecords.blm.gov first. ([Oklahoma Land Records — Land Run and Homestead Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run))
- **Search the newspaper for the homestead proof publication.** Settlers were legally required to publish their final proof notice in a local newspaper before submitting the claim. These notices name the claimant, the witnesses, and the legal description of the land. Search Gateway to Oklahoma History (gateway.okhistory.org) for free access to territorial newspapers.
- **The 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census is unique.** Because the 1890 federal census was destroyed, the surviving Oklahoma Territory special census at the Oklahoma Historical Society is one of the only windows into the 1889–1900 population. Contact OHS directly for access.
- **Trace the settler's departure state before searching Oklahoma.** Most Land Run families came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and Arkansas. The Oklahoma records document their arrival; the departure-state records document their origins, parents, and earlier vital events. Work backward through the 1900 Oklahoma census (which shows birthplace and birthplace of parents), then search the departure state. ([Oklahoma Territorial Records — Territorial Courts and Early Settlement](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts))
- **Dual-jurisdiction rule: eastern vs. western Oklahoma.** A family in western Oklahoma (Oklahoma Territory) generated territorial court and General Land Office records. A family in eastern Oklahoma (Indian Territory) generated tribal court records, BIA agency records, and Dawes Commission enrollment records. These are in different record groups at NARA. Determine which territory your ancestor lived in before selecting repositories.
- **Dawes enrollment files are the key record for Five Civilized Tribes and Freedmen ancestry.** The enrollment jackets at NARA Fort Worth (partially digitized at FamilySearch as a browse-only volume) contain family group information not found anywhere else. Even families with only partial Native American or Freedmen ancestry should check these rolls, as applications were filed by many who ultimately were not enrolled. ([Oklahoma Vital Records — Registration History](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records#Registration_History))
- **Vital registration compliance was poor even after 1908.** Oklahoma statewide vital registration began in October 1908, but the FamilySearch Wiki notes compliance was poor until the 1930s. A missing birth or death certificate before 1930 should not be taken as proof the event did not occur — seek church records, obituaries, and census records as corroboration. ([Oklahoma Vital Records — Registration History](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records#Registration_History))
- **Civil War pension files document family composition.** Many Land Run settlers were Civil War veterans or widows. Pension files in NARA contain marriage dates, names of children, and correspondence across decades — often more detailed than any vital record.
- **County tax rolls substitute for census gaps.** County personal property and real property rolls survive from 1890 onward at the Oklahoma Historical Society and are among the few annual records documenting presence in a county during the 1890s.

---

---

Researchers tracing Land Run families in Oklahoma will find that the 1889–1907 territorial era is well-documented in federal land and court records but has almost no civil vital registration — birth and death records simply did not exist as a legal requirement until 1908, and even then compliance was unreliable for decades. The single most important record class for this era is the homestead file: the application, the published newspaper proof notice, and the final proof affidavit together can establish a family's composition, ages, and witnesses. For any family with connections to eastern Oklahoma (Indian Territory), the Dawes Commission enrollment files at the National Archives in Fort Worth are equally essential and follow a completely separate administrative chain from the territorial records. Major physical repositories are the Oklahoma Historical Society in Oklahoma City (territorial censuses, tax rolls, newspapers, town histories) and NARA at Fort Worth (territorial court records, Dawes files, BIA records).

The recommended next step is to identify which of Oklahoma's two territorial halves your specific ancestor lived in, then build a targeted research plan starting with homestead records and the surviving 1890 special census before moving to church, newspaper, and tax sources.

---

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (c. 1780–1819)

## Jurisdiction Overview

The Alabama Territory was carved from the Mississippi Territory on **March 3, 1817**, and became the **State of Alabama on December 14, 1819**. For the period around 1800, researchers are actually working within the **Mississippi Territory** — and, for the Mobile Bay area, within **Spanish West Florida** (1780–1813). This multi-sovereign history is the defining research challenge.

**Four sovereign layers for the Mobile district alone:**
| Period | Sovereign | Language of records |
|---|---|---|
| 1702–1763 | French | French |
| 1763–1780 | British | English |
| 1780–1813 | Spanish | Spanish |
| 1813 onward | American | English |

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)
- **No civil registration** of births or deaths existed in this period at any level.
- **Marriage bonds and licenses** were recorded county-by-county as counties formed: Washington County (c. 1800) and Madison County (c. 1808) are the earliest.
- FamilySearch collection **"Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950"** (id 1598408; 612,345 records, 306,172 images) is the earliest digitized/indexed marriage material online. Pre-1809 coverage is sparse online — records are largely at ADAH on microfilm.

### Church Records
- **Catholic** records (Mobile, continuously from 1702) — the most complete vital-style records for this period.
- **Methodist and Baptist** from the late 1700s–early 1800s.
- FamilySearch collection **"Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950"** (id 1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images), but pre-statehood coverage within it is thin.
- **Where held:** Catholic originals (French period) → Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France. Spanish period originals → Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville; copies at the Library of Congress. American-period Catholic records → Archdiocese of Mobile Archives.

### Census Records
- The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** covering present-day Alabama. These are held at **ADAH in Montgomery — not fully digitized or name-indexed online.**
- The **1810 federal census** (first to cover the Alabama district) is indexed and online at FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- FamilySearch index: **"Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890"** (id 2016756; 287,634 records — index only, no images).
- FamilySearch index: **"Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890"** (id 1927171; 198,340 records — index only, no images).

### Probate and Court Records
- Washington County (from 1800) and Madison County (from 1808) hold the earliest county-level probate.
- FamilySearch: **"Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985"** (id 1537764; 438,210 records, 219,105 images).
- For the pre-statehood territorial period: **"Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920"** (id 1855293; 245,670 records, 122,835 images) — a key collection for 1799–1817.

### Land Records
- Alabama is a **federal-land state** (rectangular survey system).
- **St. Stephens Land Office** (opened 1807, south Alabama) and **Huntsville Land Office** (opened 1811, north Alabama) issued original patents → searchable free at **glorecords.blm.gov**.
- **"Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907"** (id 1919694; 312,450 records, 156,225 images) covers land entries for the Alabama district before statehood — important for documenting settlers' arrival.
- Spanish and British land grants for the Mobile area: originals at AGI Seville, copies at the Library of Congress.

### Military Records
- **Creek War (1813–1814)** and **War of 1812** service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants at NARA; indexed on **Fold3** (fold3.com).
- **Creek War pension files** are among the richest biographical sources: they routinely contain birth dates, marriage dates, and children's names.
- Territorial militia rolls: at ADAH.

### Tax Records
- Washington County (c. 1800) and Madison County (c. 1809) county tax lists on **ADAH microfilm**.
- **Critical workaround:** The 1801, 1805, and 1808 territorial censuses are not accessible online. County tax lists are often the only way to document a person's presence in the intercensal years before 1810.

---

## Are There Digitized, Browsable Volumes?

The agent specifically searched for browse-able digitized image volumes for the Alabama / Mississippi Territory area in the 1780–1820 window. **The result was zero named volume-level browse sets** in FamilySearch's volume catalog for this window. This is a genuine gap — not a search error.

What *does* exist with images are indexed collections (listed above), the earliest beginning around 1798–1809. You can view images within those collections, but you cannot page through unindexed volumes the way you can with some later record sets.

**Bottom line on browsable volumes:** For this place and period, FamilySearch does not offer the kind of unindexed image browsing you might do with, say, a later county deed book. Access is either through indexed collections online or through microfilm at ADAH.

---

## Records NOT Online (Require Physical or Microfilm Access)

- Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 → **ADAH, Montgomery**
- Most pre-1809 county deed books and court minutes → ADAH microfilm
- Spanish colonial census returns and land grants (Mobile district) → AGI Seville; copies at Library of Congress
- French colonial Mobile records → ANOM, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives
- Early Catholic parish registers for Mobile (pre-American period) → Archdiocese of Mobile Archives
- County tax lists for Washington County (c. 1800–1808) and Madison County (c. 1809–1817) → ADAH microfilm

---

## Key Research Tips

1. **Work the Mississippi Territory first.** For any pre-1817 event in present-day Alabama, the controlling jurisdiction is the Mississippi Territory. Search FamilySearch's Mississippi territorial and county collections alongside Alabama ones.
2. **Mobile is a separate research environment.** Pre-1813 Mobile requires Spanish and French archives — different languages, different repositories, different finding aids entirely.
3. **Use BLM GLO for land patents.** The first documentation of most interior settlers is their federal land entry or patent → free at glorecords.blm.gov.
4. **Tax lists substitute for missing census years.** The 1801, 1805, and 1808 territorial censuses are not reliably accessible online; ADAH tax-list microfilm fills the gap.
5. **Creek War pension files are a goldmine.** Searchable on Fold3; contain birth dates, marriage dates, and children's names.
6. **Trace migrants back to origin states.** Most settlers came overland from Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, or Tennessee. When Alabama records are sparse, look for the family in Georgia records — especially just before they crossed into the Alabama region.
7. **Check the PARES portal** (pares.culturaydeporte.gob.es) for any digitized AGI material before planning a trip to Seville.

---

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (c. 1780-1819)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** The Alabama Territory was carved from the Mississippi Territory on March 3, 1817, and became the State of Alabama on December 14, 1819.
- **Administrative center:** St. Stephens (territorial capital); Huntsville briefly served as early capital.
- **Parent jurisdictions:** Mississippi Territory (1798-1817); before that, Spanish West Florida (Mobile district, 1780-1813), British West Florida (1763-1780), and French Louisiana (Mobile district, 1702-1763).
- **Population during period:** The 1810 federal census counted approximately 9,046 free persons in the Madison County district (present-day north Alabama); the Mobile/Washington County area added several thousand more. By 1820 (first Alabama state census) the total population was roughly 127,901, including enslaved persons.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur and skin trade, cotton cultivation beginning to expand after the Creek War (1813-1814); Mobile was a commercial port.
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American settlers from the Carolinas, Virginia, Georgia, and Tennessee; French Creole families in the Mobile area; significant enslaved African population; Creek and Cherokee nations throughout the interior.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuits, Baptist congregations (both arrived in the late 18th century); Catholic parish at Mobile (French and Spanish colonial era, continuing through the period); Presbyterian missions.
- **Key historical events:** Spanish cession of Mobile (1813); Creek War (1813-1814), which opened the interior to rapid American settlement; Mississippi Territory division and Alabama Territory creation (1817); statehood (1819).

## Boundary changes

This is a temporally complex jurisdiction:

- **1702-1763:** Mobile district administered as part of French Louisiana.
- **1763-1780:** British West Florida (Mobile district).
- **1780-1813:** Spanish West Florida; Mobile was Spanish until the United States seized it in April 1813.
- **1798-1817:** The American Mississippi Territory was created; it originally did not include the Mobile strip (still Spanish), but was expanded north and eventually east. Present-day Alabama was entirely within the Mississippi Territory by 1812.
- **1817:** Mississippi Territory divided — the eastern half became the Alabama Territory.
- **1819:** Alabama achieved statehood.

County formation within the territory was rapid. Washington County (1800) and Madison County (1808) were among the first counties organized in present-day Alabama under the Mississippi Territory. Records for events before a county's formation are held under the parent county or at the territorial level.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Alabama did not have statewide civil registration of births and deaths during this period. No territorial-era statewide vital registration system existed.
- **What exists:** Marriage bonds and licenses were recorded at the county level as counties formed (Washington County from 1800, Madison County from 1808). FamilySearch has a statewide collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950" (collection 1598408; 612,345 records, 306,172 images) beginning at 1809 — this is the earliest indexed marriage material for the region.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (which also held marriage records); originals are at individual county courthouses or the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery.
- **Gaps:** No birth or death registration for this period. The 1809 start of the marriages collection leaves the 1800-1808 window with very sparse coverage. Pre-1800 marriages (Spanish/colonial period) were recorded only by the Catholic Church in Mobile.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic church registers in Mobile; Baptist and Methodist congregation membership rolls; wills and inventories that name surviving spouses and children.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, continuously from French period); Methodist (circuits established late 1700s in Georgia-Alabama borderlands); Baptist (congregations organized in the Tombigbee and Tennessee Valley areas by the early 1800s); Presbyterian (later, from c. 1810s).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (Catholic); membership rolls, minutes, baptisms (Methodist and Baptist).
- **Where held:** Catholic records for Mobile are held by the Archdiocese of Mobile; French originals are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France, with microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Spanish colonial church records are at the Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. FamilySearch has an "Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950" collection (1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images) beginning at 1803 — but the pre-statehood coverage within it is limited.
- **Language:** Catholic records from the French period are in French; Spanish period records are in Spanish.

### Census records
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery. Per the FamilySearch wiki search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records), these are not fully digitized and name-indexed online.
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census covered the Mississippi Territory including present-day Alabama. The 1820 federal census was the first taken after statehood.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890" (collection 2016756; 287,634 records, no images) — index only, no images attached; begins at 1810.
- **Mississippi-side substitutes:** FamilySearch also holds "Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890" (collection 1927171; 198,340 records, no images), which covers territorial-era enumerations that may include settlers who later moved into present-day Alabama.
- **Access:** The federal 1810 and 1820 census images are on Ancestry and FamilySearch (indexed). The territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 are largely physical-only or microfilm at ADAH.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships; county court minutes recording road orders, indigent relief, and assessments.
- **Date range:** County-level probate begins as each county was formed (Washington County, 1800; Madison County, 1808; etc.). FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985" (1537764; 438,210 records, 219,105 images) begins at 1809.
- **Territorial court records:** Mississippi Territory county court records are in the FamilySearch collection "Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920" (1855293; 245,670 records, 122,835 images), beginning at 1799 — this covers the territorial-era courts whose jurisdiction included present-day Alabama counties.
- **Where held:** County probate courts; ADAH has microfilm copies of many county records.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Alabama is a federal-land state — land was distributed by the U.S. government, not by the state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The U.S. General Land Office issued patents. The Huntsville Land Office (opened 1811) and the St. Stephens Land Office (opened 1807) served the Alabama district. Original patents are searchable at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office website: glorecords.blm.gov.
- **Colonial-era grants:** Spanish and British land grants in the Mobile area predate U.S. land distribution. Spanish grants are documented at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville); copies are at the Library of Congress. The FamilySearch wiki search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) confirms this.
- **Territorial-era land records:** FamilySearch holds "Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907" (1919694; 312,450 records, 156,225 images, beginning 1798) — this covers the Mississippi Territory period and includes land entries for the Alabama district.
- **Types:** Warrants, entries, patents, deeds, tax lists.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO (online, free) for federal patents; county deed books at county courthouses; ADAH for territorial records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813-1814); War of 1812 (Gulf Coast operations, including the Battle of Mobile, 1813); militia service throughout the territorial period.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants; territorial militia rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (service records and pension files); Fold3 has digitized and indexed many War of 1812 and Creek War military records. Territorial militia rolls are at ADAH.
- **Bounty land:** Veterans of the Creek War and War of 1812 could claim federal bounty land warrants — these are separate from pension files and are at NARA.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Church cemeteries associated with the earliest Catholic, Baptist, and Methodist congregations; family burial grounds on farmsteads (common in the rural interior).
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Alabama cemeteries, including some pre-statehood burials, but rural and family plots are significantly underrepresented for this early period.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are sparse or nonexistent for this period; burial documentation is mainly through church registers (Catholic) and headstone inscriptions.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Mobile Centinel (founded 1811) is among the earliest newspapers in the region. The Huntsville Republican (founded 1816) served the north Alabama settlement area.
- **Where held:** ADAH holds microfilm collections of early Alabama newspapers. Newspapers.com and Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) have some early Alabama papers, but coverage before 1819 is sparse.
- **Content value:** Legal notices (land sales, estate settlements, runaway slave advertisements), marriage notices, and public announcements.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf Coast); New Orleans (for goods and some migrants traveling up the rivers).
- **Record types:** For this early period, passenger lists are extremely sparse. Naturalization records (declarations of intention, petitions) were filed in territorial and county courts; pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record.
- **Where held:** NARA; territorial court records at ADAH. Spanish colonial passport records for Mobile are at the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Migration note:** The vast majority of settlers in the 1800-1819 period arrived overland from Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, and Tennessee — not by sea. Documenting them means tracing their origins in those states' records.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county property tax lists, poll tax lists.
- **Date range:** Washington County tax lists begin around 1800; Madison County from 1809.
- **Where held:** ADAH (microfilm); some county courthouses. Tax lists are a critical substitute for the sparse census record for 1801-1809.
- **Substitute value:** Because no statewide census was taken in 1805 or 1808 at the federal level, territorial tax lists and censuses are the primary way to document an individual's presence in the Alabama region in those years.

### Other record types
- **Territorial legislative records:** Laws and assembly journals of the Mississippi Territory and Alabama Territory name individuals in petitions and private acts. ADAH holds these.
- **Indian trade licenses and treaty records:** For researchers with Creek or Cherokee ancestry, treaty records and trade license files are at NARA (Record Group 75, Office of Indian Affairs).
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century published histories (e.g., Albert J. Pickett's "History of Alabama," 1851) preserve transcriptions of early records and biographical sketches. Available through WorldCat and ADAH.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages 1809-1950 (1598408); Alabama, Probate Records 1809-1985 (1537764); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index 1810-1890 (2016756); Alabama, Church Records 1803-1950 (1986396); Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records 1798-1907 (1919694); Mississippi, County Court Records 1799-1920 (1855293); Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes 1792-1890 (1927171) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1810, 1820); War of 1812 service and pension records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records — Creek War, War of 1812, territorial militia | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents from St. Stephens and Huntsville Land Offices (from 1807/1811) | Free |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| Chronicling America (Library of Congress) | Early Alabama newspapers (sparse pre-1819) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 0 digitized volume-level records for both "Alabama, United States" and "Mississippi Territory, United States" within the 1780-1820 date window. This is a genuine coverage gap for browse-only digitized volumes in FamilySearch's system for this pre-statehood period — it does not mean no records exist, but it means FamilySearch has not yet surfaced named volume-level digitized images for this jurisdiction and period that can be browsed through its catalog-browse interface. The collections listed above (via `collections_search`) do include images (e.g., 306,172 images in the marriages collection; 156,225 in the Mississippi land records collection), but they start at 1803-1809, not earlier.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); militia rolls; county deed and probate microfilm; early newspaper microfilm; legislative records | In-person; some microfilm loan; online catalog at archives.alabama.gov |
| County courthouses (Washington, Madison, etc.) | Original deed books, marriage bonds, probate files | In-person or mail request |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic parish registers (Mobile, from French period) | Contact request |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | French and Spanish colonial record microfilm | In-person |
| NARA (Washington, D.C. / Atlanta Federal Records Center) | Creek War and War of 1812 service/pension files; territorial court records; Indian Affairs records (RG 75) | In-person; microfilm; online via Fold3/Ancestry |
| Library of Congress | Copies of Spanish colonial records from AGI Seville | In-person; some digital via loc.gov |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records (Mobile district): census returns, church registers, land grants, passports | In-person or contact request; some digitization via PARES portal |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | Original French colonial records for Mobile (1702-1763) | In-person or contact request |

## Records NOT online

- Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (held physically at ADAH; not fully digitized or name-indexed online)
- Most pre-1809 county-level deed books and court minutes (microfilm at ADAH; not digitized online)
- Spanish colonial census returns and land grants for the Mobile district (originals at AGI Seville; copies at Library of Congress)
- French colonial Mobile records (originals at ANOM, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives)
- Territorial militia rolls (at ADAH)
- Early Catholic parish registers for Mobile prior to American period (held by Archdiocese of Mobile; not digitized online)

## Known record losses

- The Creek War of 1813-1814 caused destruction and displacement that disrupted local record-keeping in the interior.
- Many early county courthouse records from this period are fragmentary; some counties did not begin systematic record-keeping until after statehood (1819).
- Spanish records that remained locally in Mobile were partially scattered after the U.S. took possession in 1813 — a significant portion is at AGI Seville rather than in Alabama.
- No known catastrophic courthouse fire specifically for this pre-statehood period is documented in the tool results, but record survival for 1800-1817 at the county level is extremely uneven.

## Research tips

- **Work the Mississippi Territory first.** For any event before 1817 in present-day Alabama, the controlling jurisdiction is the Mississippi Territory. Search FamilySearch's Mississippi territorial and county collections (1919694, 1855293, 1927171) alongside Alabama collections — the two jurisdictions form one continuous record trail, not two separate ones. Source: FamilySearch wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records
- **Mobile is a different research environment from the rest of Alabama.** Events in the Mobile Bay area before 1813 are in Spanish and French colonial records, not American territorial records. Treat Mobile as a separate research problem requiring Spanish and French archive access. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records
- **Use the BLM GLO website for land patents.** Alabama is a federal-land state; the first documentation of most settlers in the interior is their federal land entry or patent, searchable free at glorecords.blm.gov.
- **Tax lists substitute for missing census years.** The 1801, 1805, and 1808 territorial censuses are not reliably accessible online. County tax lists from Washington and Madison Counties (ADAH microfilm) are often the only way to document an individual's presence in those intercensal years.
- **The Creek War pension files are a rich source.** Creek War veterans and their widows filed pension applications that contain biographical detail (birth date, marriage date, children's names). These are at NARA and are searchable on Fold3.
- **Trace migrants back to their origin states.** Most settlers who arrived in Alabama before 1819 came from Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, or Tennessee overland. When Alabama records are sparse, document the family in those origin-state records first (especially Georgia, which borders Alabama directly).
- **Check Georgia records for events just before Alabama arrival.** Georgia's state and county records often capture families in the years immediately before they crossed into the Alabama region; searches should extend across the state line.
- **Published county and local histories.** Albert J. Pickett's 1851 "History of Alabama" and later county histories often transcribe early records that no longer survive in original form. WorldCat and ADAH can identify relevant titles.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (c. 1780-1819)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** The Alabama Territory was carved from the Mississippi Territory on March 3, 1817, and became the State of Alabama on December 14, 1819.
- **Administrative center:** St. Stephens served as the territorial capital; Huntsville was briefly the seat of early state government.
- **Parent jurisdictions:** Mississippi Territory (1798-1817); before that, Spanish West Florida (Mobile district, 1780-1813), British West Florida (1763-1780), and French Louisiana (Mobile district, 1702-1763).
- **Population during period:** The 1810 federal census counted approximately 9,046 free persons in the Madison County district (north Alabama); the Mobile/Washington County area added several thousand more. By the 1820 state census, total population was roughly 127,901, including enslaved persons.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur and skin trade, cotton cultivation expanding rapidly after the Creek War (1813-1814); Mobile was an active Gulf Coast commercial port.
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American settlers arriving overland from the Carolinas, Virginia, Georgia, and Tennessee; French Creole families concentrated in the Mobile area; a substantial enslaved African population; Creek and Cherokee nations throughout the interior.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (Mobile, continuously from the French colonial period); Methodist circuits (established in the late 1700s along the Georgia-Alabama borderlands); Baptist congregations (organized in the Tombigbee and Tennessee Valley areas by the early 1800s); Presbyterian missions (from c. 1810s).
- **Key historical events:** U.S. seizure of Mobile from Spain (1813); Creek War (1813-1814), which broke Creek resistance and opened the interior to rapid American settlement; Mississippi Territory division and Alabama Territory creation (1817); statehood (December 14, 1819).

## Boundary changes

This is a jurisdictionally layered place that requires distinguishing two different types of split:

**Temporal succession (Mobile district):** Mobile passed through four sovereign powers in sequence — French (1702-1763), British (1763-1780), Spanish (1780-1813), American (1813 onward). Each transition produced a clean before/after rule: records before 1763 are French; 1763-1780 are British; 1780-1813 are Spanish; after 1813 are American. There is no geographic ambiguity — it is the same territory renamed and re-parented on known dates.

**Territorial division (Mississippi Territory, 1817):** In 1817 the Mississippi Territory was split along roughly the current state line — the western half became the State of Mississippi, the eastern half became the Alabama Territory. This was a geographic split: a deed, court record, or tax entry from before 1817 was filed under the Mississippi Territory, and which successor state it effectively "belongs to" now depends on which county within the old territory created it. Counties that sat entirely in present-day Alabama remain in Alabama repositories; those that straddled the line may have records in both. When researching a family event before 1817, identify which county within the Mississippi Territory it occurred in, then check that county's current state location.

**County formation:** County formation within the territory was rapid:
- Washington County formed 1800 (first Alabama-area county; covered most of south Alabama)
- Madison County formed 1808 (north Alabama)
- Additional counties formed rapidly after 1816

Records for events before a county's formation are held under the parent county or at the territorial level. Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) can advise on which county held jurisdiction for a given place at a given date.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** There was no civil registration of births or deaths in the Alabama region during this period at any level — territorial, county, or otherwise. Marriage bonds and licenses were recorded at the county level as counties formed, beginning with Washington County around 1800 and Madison County around 1808.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950" (id 1598408; 612,345 indexed records, 306,172 images) is the earliest digitized and indexed marriage material for the region. The 1800-1808 window has very sparse online coverage — county records from that window are largely at ADAH on microfilm.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (which recorded marriages); originals at individual county courthouses or ADAH, Montgomery.
- **Gaps:** No birth or death registration for this period. Pre-1800 marriages in the Mobile area were recorded only by the Catholic Church under French and Spanish administration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic church registers at Mobile; Baptist and Methodist membership rolls; wills and inventories naming surviving spouses and children; guardianship petitions that establish parental relationships.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, continuously from 1702); Methodist circuits (from late 1700s); Baptist (Tombigbee and Tennessee Valley, from early 1800s); Presbyterian (from c. 1810s).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (Catholic); membership rolls, minutes, baptisms (Methodist and Baptist).
- **Where held:** Catholic records for Mobile are held by the Archdiocese of Mobile Archives. French-period originals are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France, with microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Spanish colonial church registers are at the Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950" (id 1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images) covers from 1803 onward, but pre-statehood coverage within it is limited.
- **Language:** Catholic records from the French period are in French; Spanish period records are in Spanish. Researchers must be able to read those languages or obtain translation assistance.

### Census records

- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at ADAH in Montgomery. Per the FamilySearch wiki search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records), they are not fully digitized and name-indexed online — access requires visiting or corresponding with ADAH.
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census covered the Mississippi Territory, including present-day Alabama. The 1820 federal census was the first taken after statehood.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890" (id 2016756; 287,634 records, no images attached) — this is an index only with no viewable images; it begins at 1810. "Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890" (id 1927171; 198,340 records, no images) covers territorial-era enumerations from 1792 onward that may include settlers who later moved into present-day Alabama.
- **Access level:** The 1810 and 1820 federal census images are indexed and online at FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1801, 1805, and 1808 territorial censuses are largely physical-only or microfilm at ADAH — **browse-only at best, physical-only in practice**.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships; county court minutes recording road orders, indigent relief payments, and local assessments (which name ordinary people who never appeared in any suit).
- **Date range:** County-level probate begins as each county was formed (Washington County, 1800; Madison County, 1808). FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985" (id 1537764; 438,210 records, 219,105 images) begins at 1809.
- **Territorial court records:** FamilySearch collection "Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920" (id 1855293; 245,670 records, 122,835 images), beginning at 1799, covers territorial-era courts whose jurisdiction included the Alabama district before statehood. This is a key collection for the 1799-1817 period.
- **Where held:** County probate courts; ADAH holds microfilm copies of many county records.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Alabama is a federal-land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The U.S. General Land Office issued the original patents. The St. Stephens Land Office (opened 1807, serving south Alabama) and the Huntsville Land Office (opened 1811, serving north Alabama) are the relevant federal offices. Patents are searchable free at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office website: glorecords.blm.gov.
- **Colonial-era grants:** Spanish and British land grants in the Mobile area predate U.S. land distribution. Spanish grants are at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville), with copies at the Library of Congress. Per the FamilySearch wiki search (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records), French colonial records are at ANOM, Aix-en-Provence.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907" (id 1919694; 312,450 records, 156,225 images, from 1798) covers the Mississippi Territory period and includes land entries for the Alabama district — this is an important collection for documenting arrival of settlers before statehood.
- **Types:** Warrants, entries, patents, deeds, tax lists, pre-emption claims.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO (online, free) for federal patents; county deed books at county courthouses; ADAH for territorial records.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813-1814); War of 1812 (Gulf Coast operations, including the Battle of Mobile, 1813); territorial militia service throughout the period.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants, and territorial militia rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C., and Atlanta) for service records and pension files. Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) has digitized and indexed many War of 1812 and Creek War records. Territorial militia rolls are at ADAH.
- **Bounty land:** Veterans of the Creek War and War of 1812 could claim federal bounty land warrants — these are separate from pension files and are at NARA.
- **Pension files as a research tool:** Creek War pension files submitted by veterans and their widows routinely contain birth dates, marriage dates, and children's names — among the richest biographical sources for this population.

### Cemetery records

- **Major cemeteries:** Church cemeteries associated with the earliest Catholic, Baptist, and Methodist congregations; family burial grounds on farmsteads (extremely common in the rural interior).
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Alabama cemeteries, including some pre-statehood burials, but rural and family plots are significantly underrepresented for this early period.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are sparse or nonexistent for this period. Documentation is mainly through Catholic church registers (for Mobile) and headstone inscriptions, many of which have been transcribed by local genealogical societies.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The Mobile Centinel (founded 1811) is among the earliest newspapers in the region. The Huntsville Republican (founded 1816) served the north Alabama settlement area.
- **Where held:** ADAH holds microfilm of early Alabama newspapers. Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) has some early Alabama papers, but coverage before 1819 is sparse. Newspapers.com has additional holdings.
- **Content value:** Legal notices (land sales, estate settlements), marriage notices, and runaway slave advertisements that name enslaved persons and owners.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf Coast); New Orleans (for goods and migrants traveling up the river systems).
- **Record types:** Passenger lists for this early period are extremely sparse for the Gulf Coast. Naturalization records (declarations of intention, petitions) were filed in territorial and county courts; pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record and are scattered across NARA and ADAH. Spanish colonial passport records for the Mobile district are at the Archivo General de Indias.
- **Migration note:** The vast majority of settlers in the 1800-1819 period arrived overland from Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, and Tennessee — not by sea. Documenting them means tracing origins in those states' records rather than seeking ship manifests. Examine family groups on passenger manifests when relevant — children as young as newborns are listed.
- **Content note:** For the earlier Spanish colonial period, the AGI holds a series of census returns and militia lists for the Mobile district that function similarly to later census enumerations.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Territorial and county property tax lists, poll tax lists.
- **Date range:** Washington County tax lists from around 1800; Madison County from around 1809.
- **Where held:** ADAH (microfilm); some county courthouses.
- **Substitute value:** Because no federal census was taken in 1805 or 1808, and the territorial censuses of those years are largely not accessible online, county tax lists are frequently the only way to document an individual's presence in the Alabama region in the intercensal years. They are a primary workaround for the gap between the 1800 and 1810 federal censuses.

### Other record types

- **Territorial legislative records:** Laws and assembly journals of the Mississippi Territory and Alabama Territory name individuals in petitions and private acts. ADAH holds these and they are indexed in part through published volumes.
- **Indian Affairs records:** For researchers with Creek or Cherokee ancestry, treaty records, trade license files, and removal records are at NARA, Record Group 75 (Office of Indian Affairs). These records also name white traders and agents.
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century published local histories (Albert J. Pickett's "History of Alabama," 1851, is the foundational one) preserve transcriptions of early records and biographical sketches — often the only surviving transcription of records since lost. Available through WorldCat and ADAH.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

It does not mean no records exist — the `collections_search` results above do include images (for example, 156,225 images in the Mississippi territorial land records collection and 122,835 in the county court records collection), but these collections begin at 1798-1809 and are searched as indexed collections rather than browsable volumes. The specific record-type collections listed are the best online access points.

## Records NOT online

- Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (physical at ADAH; not fully digitized or name-indexed online)
- Most pre-1809 county-level deed books and court minutes (microfilm at ADAH; not digitized online)
- Spanish colonial census returns and land grants for the Mobile district (originals at AGI Seville; copies at Library of Congress — not fully digitized online)
- French colonial Mobile records (originals at ANOM, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives)
- Territorial militia rolls (at ADAH)
- Early Catholic parish registers for Mobile prior to the American period (held by Archdiocese of Mobile Archives; not digitized online)
- County tax lists for Washington County (c. 1800-1808) and Madison County (c. 1809-1817) — microfilm at ADAH

## Known record losses

- The Creek War of 1813-1814 caused destruction and population displacement that disrupted local record-keeping in the interior counties.
- Many early county courthouse records from this period are fragmentary; some counties did not begin systematic record-keeping until after statehood in 1819.
- Spanish records that remained locally in Mobile were partially dispersed after the U.S. took possession in 1813 — a significant portion is now at AGI Seville rather than in Alabama repositories.
- Record survival for 1800-1817 at the county level is extremely uneven across Washington, Madison, and other early counties.

## Research tips

- **Work the Mississippi Territory first.** For any event before 1817 in present-day Alabama, the controlling jurisdiction is the Mississippi Territory. Search FamilySearch's Mississippi territorial and county collections (ids 1919694, 1855293, 1927171) alongside Alabama collections — the two jurisdictions form one continuous record trail. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records
- **Mobile is a separate research environment.** Events in the Mobile Bay area before 1813 are in Spanish and French colonial records, not American territorial records. Treat pre-1813 Mobile as requiring Spanish and French archive access — different languages, different repositories, different finding aids. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records
- **Use the BLM GLO website for land patents.** Alabama is a federal-land state; the first documentation of most settlers in the interior is their federal land entry or patent, searchable free at glorecords.blm.gov.
- **Tax lists substitute for missing census years.** The 1801, 1805, and 1808 territorial censuses are not reliably accessible online. County tax lists from Washington and Madison Counties (ADAH microfilm) are often the only way to document an individual's presence in those intercensal years.
- **The Creek War pension files are a rich source.** Veterans and their widows filed pension applications that contain birth dates, marriage dates, and children's names — among the richest biographical sources for this population. Searchable on Fold3.
- **Trace migrants back to their origin states.** Most settlers who arrived in Alabama before 1819 came overland from Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, or Tennessee. When Alabama records are sparse, document the family in origin-state records — especially Georgia, which borders Alabama directly. Georgia records often capture a family in the years immediately before they crossed into the Alabama region.
- **Published county and territorial histories.** Albert J. Pickett's 1851 "History of Alabama" and subsequent county histories often transcribe early records that no longer survive in original form. WorldCat (worldcat.org) and ADAH can identify relevant titles.
- **PARES portal for Spanish colonial records.** The Spanish government's PARES portal (pares.culturaydeporte.gob.es) has digitized some Archivo General de Indias materials; it is worth checking before planning a trip to Seville.

---

The Alabama region around 1800 presents one of the more layered pre-statehood research environments in the United States. The territory was under four different sovereign powers before it became a U.S. state in 1819, which means records fall into dramatically different repositories depending on both where and when an event occurred. The Mobile Bay area before 1813 is essentially a European colonial research problem requiring Spanish and French archives; the interior north and east Alabama counties from 1800 onward are an American territorial problem rooted in the Mississippi Territory's records, which are held partly at the Alabama Department of Archives and History in Montgomery and partly in FamilySearch's Mississippi-labeled collections online. No digitized, browse-able volume-level records for this specific pre-statehood window appeared in FamilySearch's volume catalog, but several indexed collections with images do begin as early as 1798-1809, covering territorial land records, county court records, marriages, and church records. The biggest practical warning is that the territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 — the main head-of-household lists for the intercensal years — are not online and require contacting ADAH directly; county tax lists on ADAH microfilm are the workaround.

The next step would be to build a targeted research plan using this survey as its foundation — identifying which specific families and events to pursue and in which record sets to begin.

# Locality Guide: Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood (c. 1780-1819)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** The Alabama Territory was carved from the Mississippi Territory on March 3, 1817, and became the State of Alabama on December 14, 1819.
- **Administrative center:** St. Stephens (territorial capital); Huntsville briefly served as early capital.
- **Parent jurisdictions:** Mississippi Territory (1798-1817); before that, Spanish West Florida (Mobile district, 1780-1813), British West Florida (1763-1780), and French Louisiana (Mobile district, 1702-1763).
- **Population during period:** The 1810 federal census counted approximately 9,046 free persons in the Madison County district (present-day north Alabama); the Mobile/Washington County area added several thousand more. By 1820 (first Alabama state census) the total population was roughly 127,901, including enslaved persons.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur and skin trade, cotton cultivation beginning to expand after the Creek War (1813-1814); Mobile was a commercial port.
- **Ethnic composition:** Anglo-American settlers from the Carolinas, Virginia, Georgia, and Tennessee; French Creole families in the Mobile area; significant enslaved African population; Creek and Cherokee nations throughout the interior.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist circuits, Baptist congregations (both arrived in the late 18th century); Catholic parish at Mobile (French and Spanish colonial era, continuing through the period); Presbyterian missions.
- **Key historical events:** Spanish cession of Mobile (1813); Creek War (1813-1814), which opened the interior to rapid American settlement; Mississippi Territory division and Alabama Territory creation (1817); statehood (1819).

## Boundary changes

This is a temporally complex jurisdiction:

- **1702-1763:** Mobile district administered as part of French Louisiana.
- **1763-1780:** British West Florida (Mobile district).
- **1780-1813:** Spanish West Florida; Mobile was Spanish until the United States seized it in April 1813.
- **1798-1817:** The American Mississippi Territory was created; it originally did not include the Mobile strip (still Spanish), but was expanded north and eventually east. Present-day Alabama was entirely within the Mississippi Territory by 1812.
- **1817:** Mississippi Territory divided — the eastern half became the Alabama Territory.
- **1819:** Alabama achieved statehood.

County formation within the territory was rapid. Washington County (1800) and Madison County (1808) were among the first counties organized in present-day Alabama under the Mississippi Territory. Records for events before a county's formation are held under the parent county or at the territorial level.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Alabama did not have statewide civil registration of births and deaths during this period. No territorial-era statewide vital registration system existed.
- **What exists:** Marriage bonds and licenses were recorded at the county level as counties formed (Washington County from 1800, Madison County from 1808). FamilySearch has a statewide collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950" (collection 1598408; 612,345 records, 306,172 images) beginning at 1809 — this is the earliest indexed marriage material for the region.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (which also held marriage records); originals are at individual county courthouses or the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery.
- **Gaps:** No birth or death registration for this period. The 1809 start of the marriages collection leaves the 1800-1808 window with very sparse coverage. Pre-1800 marriages (Spanish/colonial period) were recorded only by the Catholic Church in Mobile.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic church registers in Mobile; Baptist and Methodist congregation membership rolls; wills and inventories that name surviving spouses and children.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic (Mobile, continuously from French period); Methodist (circuits established late 1700s in Georgia-Alabama borderlands); Baptist (congregations organized in the Tombigbee and Tennessee Valley areas by the early 1800s); Presbyterian (later, from c. 1810s).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials (Catholic); membership rolls, minutes, baptisms (Methodist and Baptist).
- **Where held:** Catholic records for Mobile are held by the Archdiocese of Mobile; French originals are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France, with microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Spanish colonial church records are at the Archivo General de Indias (AGI), Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. FamilySearch has an "Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950" collection (1986396; 156,789 records, 78,394 images) beginning at 1803 — but the pre-statehood coverage within it is limited.
- **Language:** Catholic records from the French period are in French; Spanish period records are in Spanish.

### Census records
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 that enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery. Per the FamilySearch wiki search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records), these are not fully digitized and name-indexed online.
- **Federal census:** The 1810 federal census covered the Mississippi Territory including present-day Alabama. The 1820 federal census was the first taken after statehood.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890" (collection 2016756; 287,634 records, no images) — index only, no images attached; begins at 1810.
- **Mississippi-side substitutes:** FamilySearch also holds "Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890" (collection 1927171; 198,340 records, no images), which covers territorial-era enumerations that may include settlers who later moved into present-day Alabama.
- **Access:** The federal 1810 and 1820 census images are on Ancestry and FamilySearch (indexed). The territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 are largely physical-only or microfilm at ADAH.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships; county court minutes recording road orders, indigent relief, and assessments.
- **Date range:** County-level probate begins as each county was formed (Washington County, 1800; Madison County, 1808; etc.). FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985" (1537764; 438,210 records, 219,105 images) begins at 1809.
- **Territorial court records:** Mississippi Territory county court records are in the FamilySearch collection "Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799-1920" (1855293; 245,670 records, 122,835 images), beginning at 1799 — this covers the territorial-era courts whose jurisdiction included present-day Alabama counties.
- **Where held:** County probate courts; ADAH has microfilm copies of many county records.

- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Alabama is a federal-land state — land was distributed by the U.S. government, not by the state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The U.S. General Land Office issued patents. The Huntsville Land Office (opened 1811) and the St. Stephens Land Office (opened 1807) served the Alabama district. Original patents are searchable at the Bureau of Land Management General Land Office website: glorecords.blm.gov.
- **Colonial-era grants:** Spanish and British land grants in the Mobile area predate U.S. land distribution. Spanish grants are documented at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville); copies are at the Library of Congress. The FamilySearch wiki search result (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) confirms this.
- **Territorial-era land records:** FamilySearch holds "Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907" (1919694; 312,450 records, 156,225 images, beginning 1798) — this covers the Mississippi Territory period and includes land entries for the Alabama district.
- **Types:** Warrants, entries, patents, deeds, tax lists.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO (online, free) for federal patents; county deed books at county courthouses; ADAH for territorial records.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813-1814); War of 1812 (Gulf Coast operations, including the Battle of Mobile, 1813); militia service throughout the territorial period.
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants; territorial militia rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (service records and pension files); Fold3 has digitized and indexed many War of 1812 and Creek War military records. Territorial militia rolls are at ADAH.
- **Bounty land:** Veterans of the Creek War and War of 1812 could claim federal bounty land warrants — these are separate from pension files and are at NARA.

### Cemetery records

- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) covers many Alabama cemeteries, including some pre-statehood burials, but rural and family plots are significantly underrepresented for this early period.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are sparse or nonexistent for this period; burial documentation is mainly through church registers (Catholic) and headstone inscriptions.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Mobile Centinel (founded 1811) is among the earliest newspapers in the region. The Huntsville Republican (founded 1816) served the north Alabama settlement area.
- **Where held:** ADAH holds microfilm collections of early Alabama newspapers. Newspapers.com and Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) have some early Alabama papers, but coverage before 1819 is sparse.
- **Content value:** Legal notices (land sales, estate settlements, runaway slave advertisements), marriage notices, and public announcements.

- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf Coast); New Orleans (for goods and some migrants traveling up the rivers).
- **Record types:** For this early period, passenger lists are extremely sparse. Naturalization records (declarations of intention, petitions) were filed in territorial and county courts; pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record.
- **Where held:** NARA; territorial court records at ADAH. Spanish colonial passport records for Mobile are at the Archivo General de Indias.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county property tax lists, poll tax lists.
- **Date range:** Washington County tax lists begin around 1800; Madison County from 1809.
- **Where held:** ADAH (microfilm); some county courthouses. Tax lists are a critical substitute for the sparse census record for 1801-1809.
- **Substitute value:** Because no statewide census was taken in 1805 or 1808 at the federal level, territorial tax lists and censuses are the primary way to document an individual's presence in the Alabama region in those years.

- **Territorial legislative records:** Laws and assembly journals of the Mississippi Territory and Alabama Territory name individuals in petitions and private acts. ADAH holds these.
- **Indian trade licenses and treaty records:** For researchers with Creek or Cherokee ancestry, treaty records and trade license files are at NARA (Record Group 75, Office of Indian Affairs).
- **Town and county histories:** 19th-century published histories (e.g., Albert J. Pickett's "History of Alabama," 1851) preserve transcriptions of early records and biographical sketches. Available through WorldCat and ADAH.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages 1809-1950 (1598408); Alabama, Probate Records 1809-1985 (1537764); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index 1810-1890 (2016756); Alabama, Church Records 1803-1950 (1986396); Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records 1798-1907 (1919694); Mississippi, County Court Records 1799-1920 (1855293); Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes 1792-1890 (1927171) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (1810, 1820); War of 1812 service and pension records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military Records — Creek War, War of 1812, territorial militia | Subscription |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents from St. Stephens and Huntsville Land Offices (from 1807/1811) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 0 digitized volume-level records for both "Alabama, United States" and "Mississippi Territory, United States" within the 1780-1820 date window. This is a genuine coverage gap for browse-only digitized volumes in FamilySearch's system for this pre-statehood period — it does not mean no records exist, but it means FamilySearch has not yet surfaced named volume-level digitized images for this jurisdiction and period that can be browsed through its catalog-browse interface. The collections listed above (via `collections_search`) do include images (e.g., 306,172 images in the marriages collection; 156,225 in the Mississippi land records collection), but they start at 1803-1809, not earlier.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); militia rolls; county deed and probate microfilm; early newspaper microfilm; legislative records | In-person; some microfilm loan; online catalog at archives.alabama.gov |
| County courthouses (Washington, Madison, etc.) | Original deed books, marriage bonds, probate files | In-person or mail request |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic parish registers (Mobile, from French period) | Contact request |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | French and Spanish colonial record microfilm | In-person |
| NARA (Washington, D.C. / Atlanta Federal Records Center) | Creek War and War of 1812 service/pension files; territorial court records; Indian Affairs records (RG 75) | In-person; microfilm; online via Fold3/Ancestry |
| Library of Congress | Copies of Spanish colonial records from AGI Seville | In-person; some digital via loc.gov |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records (Mobile district): census returns, church registers, land grants, passports | In-person or contact request; some digitization via PARES portal |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France | Original French colonial records for Mobile (1702-1763) | In-person or contact request |

## Records NOT online

- Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, and 1808 (held physically at ADAH; not fully digitized or name-indexed online)
- Most pre-1809 county-level deed books and court minutes (microfilm at ADAH; not digitized online)
- Spanish colonial census returns and land grants for the Mobile district (originals at AGI Seville; copies at Library of Congress)
- French colonial Mobile records (originals at ANOM, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives)
- Territorial militia rolls (at ADAH)
- Early Catholic parish registers for Mobile prior to American period (held by Archdiocese of Mobile; not digitized online)

## Known record losses

- The Creek War of 1813-1814 caused destruction and displacement that disrupted local record-keeping in the interior.
- Many early county courthouse records from this period are fragmentary; some counties did not begin systematic record-keeping until after statehood (1819).
- Spanish records that remained locally in Mobile were partially scattered after the U.S. took possession in 1813 — a significant portion is at AGI Seville rather than in Alabama.
- No known catastrophic courthouse fire specifically for this pre-statehood period is documented in the tool results, but record survival for 1800-1817 at the county level is extremely uneven.

## Research tips

- **Work the Mississippi Territory first.** For any event before 1817 in present-day Alabama, the controlling jurisdiction is the Mississippi Territory. Search FamilySearch's Mississippi territorial and county collections (1919694, 1855293, 1927171) alongside Alabama collections — the two jurisdictions form one continuous record trail, not two separate ones. Source: FamilySearch wiki search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records
- **Mobile is a different research environment from the rest of Alabama.** Events in the Mobile Bay area before 1813 are in Spanish and French colonial records, not American territorial records. Treat Mobile as a separate research problem requiring Spanish and French archive access. Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records
- **Use the BLM GLO website for land patents.** Alabama is a federal-land state; the first documentation of most settlers in the interior is their federal land entry or patent, searchable free at glorecords.blm.gov.
- **Tax lists substitute for missing census years.** The 1801, 1805, and 1808 territorial censuses are not reliably accessible online. County tax lists from Washington and Madison Counties (ADAH microfilm) are often the only way to document an individual's presence in those intercensal years.
- **The Creek War pension files are a rich source.** Creek War veterans and their widows filed pension applications that contain biographical detail (birth date, marriage date, children's names). These are at NARA and are searchable on Fold3.
- **Trace migrants back to their origin states.** Most settlers who arrived in Alabama before 1819 came from Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, or Tennessee overland. When Alabama records are sparse, document the family in those origin-state records first (especially Georgia, which borders Alabama directly).
- **Check Georgia records for events just before Alabama arrival.** Georgia's state and county records often capture families in the years immediately before they crossed into the Alabama region; searches should extend across the state line.
- **Published county and local histories.** Albert J. Pickett's 1851 "History of Alabama" and later county histories often transcribe early records that no longer survive in original form. WorldCat and ADAH can identify relevant titles.

Here is the locality guide returned by the subagent:

---

**Locality entry written as loc_001.**

---

## Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide (1860s–1890s)

### Counties Covered
The guide focuses on the five principal anthracite coal counties: **Schuylkill**, **Carbon**, **Luzerne**, **Northumberland**, and **Lackawanna** (the latter created in 1878 from Luzerne County).

---

### Key Finding: Specialized Coal-Region Index
The FamilySearch wiki page **"Pennsylvania Coal Region Records"** (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) was retrieved and contains real, specific content. The most important resource found there:

- **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** — names approximately **41,000 colliery workers** from surviving payroll books. This is the premier specialized index for identifying Irish miners by name.
- **Molly Maguires court records** at the Historical Society of Schuylkill County — critical for Irish labor history in the region.

---

### Vital Records
Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil vital registration** during most of this period (registration began 1906). Substitutes:
- **Catholic parish registers** are the primary source — essential for Irish immigrant families.
- **Diocese of Allentown** (formerly Philadelphia) covers Schuylkill and Carbon counties — contact their diocesan archive.
- **Diocese of Scranton** covers Lackawanna and Luzerne counties.

---

### Census Records
Standard U.S. federal censuses (1860, 1870, 1880, 1900) are available and name-indexed. Pennsylvania had no state census during this window.

---

### Naturalization Records
From the FamilySearch wiki on **Pennsylvania Naturalization Records**:
- Courts at every level (Common Pleas, District, Circuit, Supreme) could naturalize; miners often used the nearest county courthouse.
- Many declarations of intent and petitions survive at individual county courthouses and on microfilm at FamilySearch.
- No statewide index exists — searches must be run county by county.

---

### FamilySearch Digitized Holdings (Largely Unindexed)
Five digitized but **largely un-indexed** record categories exist on FamilySearch for Schuylkill County and must be browsed image by image:
1. Naturalization records
2. Church records
3. Probate records
4. Marriage records
5. Deed records

No name search is possible for these volumes — plan for **image browsing** (use the search-images agent).

---

### Critical Jurisdictional Trap
> **Lackawanna County did not exist before 1878.** All pre-1878 Scranton-area records are filed under **Luzerne County** at Wilkes-Barre. If your ancestor was in Scranton before 1878, search Luzerne County records.

---

### Suggested Research Sequence for Irish Coal Miners
1. **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** — identify the miner and his colliery.
2. **Federal census records** (1860–1900) — place the family in a specific township.
3. **Catholic parish registers** — find baptisms, marriages, and burials; use diocesan archives.
4. **County naturalization records** at the courthouse or on FamilySearch microfilm.
5. **Molly Maguires / labor court records** at Schuylkill County Historical Society (if applicable).
6. **Image-browse** the unindexed FamilySearch volumes for the relevant county.

---

### What's Still Needed
The four remaining counties — **Luzerne, Carbon, Northumberland, and Lackawanna** — each need their own separate locality survey before a complete research plan can be built. The Schuylkill County survey was the starting point written to **loc_001** in your project.

Irish surnames were frequently anglicized inconsistently across census, court, and church records — search all spelling variants (e.g. O'Brien / Brien / Bryan).
Luzerne, Carbon, Northumberland, and Lackawanna counties each require their own locality survey; this guide covers Schuylkill County only.
